items.title: Temporarily leaving to observe the changes in the field?
items.human_voice:
I am about to finish the first year of my PhD. My goal is to become a professor at a research institution, publish papers, advise students, etc. Even if that doesn't work out, (perhaps due to the competitiveness of the market or some other reason), doing a PhD is still something I want to do and I am passionate about my field.

However, I work in a very theoretical area, treading the lines between math and physics. It has become increasingly clear to me that AI will have a major impact in the way academia structures itself, including how people get hired and promoted. For this reason, I am thinking of taking a leave of absence for a year (or two?) (as allowed by my institution) to watch how the field evolves and whether various ethical dilemmas and logistical obstacles converge towards a solution. I think this would help me avoid a moving target since the metrics of success in the field have surely been changing very fast. In 2025, AI companies were announcing their models performed to the level of a talented high schooler in math. Today, they are announcing solutions to long-standing open problems in the field.
As examples of my concerns:

In a world where most people can prompt an AI model to generate a new novel result, what will be the criteria used to hire postdocs when I'm graduating 4/5 years from now? It is not too far-fetched that perhaps even post-docs will need to submit test scores to prove their competency in the field, since that would not be apparent from an applicant with a publication record of AI-assisted papers. I can't know what it will look like and it would be helpful to have some idea of it so that I can optimize for it during my time as a student.
Perhaps AI becomes the norm in the field, and everyone who doesn't use it is put at a severe disadvantage, akin to deciding not to use any computers or calculators today. In which case perhaps I would consider different career options while keeping my passion subject as a hobby, since there are not many parts of the job that I would wish to automate. I enjoy it fully.

Question: in your experience, has this strategy of "waiting it out" on a problem before making a decision or commitment paid off? Or perhaps you found more useful to go with the flow in order not to miss any unforeseen opportunities? Particularly helpful would be examples in the academic world of "disruptive moments" and the various strategies employed by different people (with their respective results), especially those involving a temporary leave. Also helpful would be pros and cons that you see in this specific situation related to the impacts of AI in academia.

Additional information: I am in the US doing theoretical physics and I have not settled onto an advisor yet. My program recommends making this decision after the second year. I am fresh out of college and fortunate enough that my parents would welcome me home for said absence (so I would not be picky about employment as long as I can afford my share of the expenses, although expecting to do something relating to education during this time).

I am hoping this can be considered a constructive subjective question, as explained in the help center.

items.title: Would it be wise to pursue a second Ph.D. given my circumstances?
items.human_voice:
I am seriously considering pursuing a second Ph.D. I have already completed my GRE general test and plan to start applying to universities shortly. I am aware that pursuing a second Ph.D. is generally not recommended for the advancement of one’s career, but I think my circumstances are relatively unique, and this may be the best course of action for my career. Still, I would like to receive advice from those familiar with academia or other R&D careers to evaluate any problems before I encounter them and before I commit to this decision.

I currently hold a Ph.D. in physics, and I am looking to obtain a Ph.D. in aerospace engineering. Now I originally was going to obtain a Ph.D. in aerospace engineering. Twenty years ago, I enrolled in a reputable aerospace engineering doctoral program after receiving a B.S. in electrical engineering and a M.S. in physics. Because of a combination of absolutely terrible academic advice and a terrible mismatch between my research interest and those of my doctoral advisors, I ultimately gave up on my aerospace engineering Ph.D., earning an M.S. aerospace engineering degree instead. I then changed institutions and went on to earn a physics Ph.D.

This is a decision I came to regret almost as soon as I switched institutions, and one which I regret to this day. Still, I committed to my Ph.D. program this time around, and in five years’ time I had earned by physics Ph.D. With Ph.D. in hand, I attempted to get back into aerospace engineering research. No post-doc aerospace related program would take me. I also could not obtain any entry level aerospace engineering positions in the private sector despite possessing an M.S. in aerospace engineering. I ultimately took a position as a physicist with a national defense research laboratory (thanks in part to connections that my doctoral advisor had), specializing in lasers, optics and directed energy.

I have been with this national lab for over ten years now. My first project with this laboratory was both ambitious and self-directed, but after five years with limited results it was canceled. I presented this project at several conferences and wrote an internal technical report on it, but I was never able to get the results published in an academic journal. After a couple of years drifting between minor projects I finally got attached to an interesting and important project with talented people. This arrangement was extremely promising, but two years into the project the budget was cut in its entirety for political reasons, and I am again drifting between minor projects I have little investment in.

After ten years of physics research, I have two failed projects under my belt, no first author publications since I left university and a few conference presentations to my name. I am paid well and my working conditions are good, but I find my current line of work unsatisfying. I can’t secure a position as a professor because of my weak publication record. I am currently searching for other R&D positions, but I have yet to have any success finding any.
This is when the idea of obtaining a second Ph.D. occurred to me. Why not go back to school and maybe undo the biggest regret in my life? My professional career is going nowhere, I have never had any success switching to aerospace engineering since receiving a physics Ph.D., and I currently have no family to tie me down. I am also relatively financially secure. As long as I can secure a teaching or research assistanceship, I should be able to make it through a Ph.D. program without any financial hardships and have plenty of savings left once I graduate.

My real concern is whether I will be treated fairly should I attempt to enroll in a Ph.D. program given my current circumstances. Would any University, or more importantly, research professors be interested in taking on a middle-aged student who already possesses a Ph.D. along with a less than stellar research career? Would I still be offered tuition assistance or a research assistanceship? Back in my twenties, when I had excellent grades and standardized test scores, I was basically guaranteed a research assistanceship wherever I went. I am not certain this will be the case in my current situation. Finally, I need someone to hire me once I complete my second Ph.D.

Would enrolling in an aerospace Ph.D. program make sense given the circumstances? What problems would you anticipate if I did this? What risk do you think I am taking? Can you suggest any better alternatives?

Thanks for reading, and for any advice you would be willing to provide.

items.title: How do speakers handle public speaking on difficult topics without your voice breaking?
items.human_voice:
I have to talk a lot in my job and am generally a confident, capable presenter - I would give many 20+ person presentations a week, a couple of 100+'s a month, and occasionally talk to live audiences as big as 20k. But sometimes, I need to give a speech that's a bit more emotional (a wedding, a funeral, a work presentation that involves a story about a dead kid...) and my voice breaks. This can happen in a meeting of 3 people, or in a venue of 100.

I've never got as far as actual tears, but it's not "aww how sweet, a little voice crack, this person cares" - it's multiple sentences struggling to speak and keep my voice level. I don't even feel consciously upset in the moment - it's just a sad story and there is some low-level part of my brain that seems incapable of recounting it without sadness. I find it embarassing and I'm sure it makes it hard for the audience to follow along.

I have found that rehearsal helps, but does not reliably eliminate, this problem. An actor recommended pressing your tongue to the roof of your mouth between sentences but this has not (for me, at least) really helped. I've heard "picture everybody in the audience doing something funny" but I find that doesn't make a difference either.

Are there other concrete techniques or tricks of the trade that people use to avoid losing it when telling a sad story or giving an emotional speech?

items.title: How do I prevent myself from coming off as stuck up or conceited when discussing personal acheivement
items.human_voice:
I work in the firearms industry and this is a field largely dominated by males. In addition, the social currency of choice is based on how impressive any given person's encyclopedic knowledge of something might be and I simply don't have that. When I started working at my current job I didn't think that would be an issue; I know quite a bit and I am no stranger to deferring to a more knowledgeable coworker. That said, in the past few months I've started to notice how that lack of technical knowledge has made other view me in a more negative or less serious light. Sometimes when a group of staff and customers are having a conversation right in front of me they include me in the way you might include a child. Sometimes I will be speaking and a coworker will interrupt and outright disregard me, even if they are about to repeat what I have already said to a customer. It's extremely frustrating because this is a retail setting that I am more than over qualified to work in. I also don't want to ascribe meaning to the stupid social currency, so on one hand I've been inclined to ignore the bad behavior of others or simply let it roll of my shoulders.

On the other hand, I feel this very egotistical urge to remind those around me of the context of my situation- my fiance makes 6 figures and I am only working here because I like guns and I need to leave the house on occasion. Additionally, my masters program is about to start and I'll be cutting my hours pretty significantly, and I have noticed that this fact has made even my boss a little touchy. I have listened to repeated digs about how successful _____ is even though they didn't go to college, as if I've ever implied it was somehow necessary.

In response, I have mostly gently inserted my own commentary about my knowledge of the industry and nothing more. I don't want to make the mistake of going on an "I'm better than you" rant that makes everyone hate me, and I don't genuinely think that I am. It's just really upsetting to be constantly disregarded as the token girl in the room, even though I'm a valuable member of the team and I know this. How do I stand up for myself, maybe even talk myself up a bit, without seeming stuck up?

items.title: When should I use GraphRAG instead of traditional vector-based RAG?
items.human_voice:
I’m building a RAG application where users ask questions over a collection of documents.

The traditional architecture I’m considering is:

Split documents into chunks

Generate embeddings

Store the embeddings in a vector database

Retrieve the top-k most similar chunks

Pass those chunks to an LLM

This works reasonably well for questions where the answer is contained in one or a few semantically similar chunks.

However, I’m running into questions that require connecting information across multiple entities or documents. For example:

“Which customers are affected by vulnerabilities in products that depend on library X?”

The relevant information may be distributed across several records:

Customer -> uses -> Product
Product -> depends_on -> Library
Library -> has -> Vulnerability

A vector search can retrieve documents mentioning the customer, product, library, or vulnerability, but it does not explicitly perform the multi-hop relationship traversal.

I’ve been looking at GraphRAG approaches where the retrieved context includes a knowledge graph and graph traversal in addition to, or instead of, vector similarity search.

My questions are:

What types of queries are a good indication that GraphRAG is preferable to standard vector RAG?

Is GraphRAG typically used as a replacement for vector retrieval, or as an additional retrieval step?

How do production GraphRAG systems decide which subgraph to retrieve without sending an excessively large graph to the LLM?

Are there established ways to measure whether GraphRAG actually improves retrieval quality compared with vector RAG, especially for multi-hop questions?

I’m particularly interested in architectural or implementation differences rather than comparisons between specific database products.

items.title: When is it safe to construct Swing objects OFF of the event queue?
items.human_voice:
I have a very simple task.

I need to query a file system for some files, filtering out the unwanted files/folders along the way.
I need to read the files, line-by-line, for a certain String, saving the line and line number for matches.
I need to take these results and construct a TreeNode, which, in turn, will be used to construct a JTree.

I am using a SwingWorker to do the task, as this is obviously IO bound and quite slow. I am parsing a large file tree -- 10k-50k files minimum, each quite large.

Anyways, I do steps 1 and 2 in the doInBackground method of SwingWorker, firing off publish calls to feed into my custom process method implementation, so that I can let the user know of their progress while they are waiting.

However, step 3 feels like it needs to be done in the done method, as that method is executed on the Event Queue Thread. I was taught as a student to NEVER EVER DO ANYTHING SWING-like OUTSIDE OF THE EVENT THREAD.

Ok, when trying to do step 3 on the done method, it works, but my attempts to call publish don't trigger updates on my loading screen panel. After some thinking, I realized that it made sense -- the done method itself is the one occupying the event thread! So how could my loading screen receive updates?!

Thus, I am stuck here, probably by false teachings.

Is it safe to construct Swing objects off of the event thread? For example, a TreeNode? And if so, what was my teacher warning us about?

Plus, when constructing this question, I saw this post about the same subject -- Is it safe to construct Swing/AWT widgets NOT on the Event Dispatch Thread?

Looks like Sun/Oracle themselves have encouraged the mentality. So, at least, my teacher isn't pulling it from nowhere.

google.script.run success/failure callback never fires intermittently (server executes fine, client hangs)
items.human_voice:
I have an HTML Service web app that calls a server-side function via google.script.run to read data from a Google Sheet:

javascript

google.script.run
.withSuccessHandler(function (p) { /* render data */ })
.withFailureHandler(function (err) { /* show error */ })
.getInvestorProfile(sessionToken);

Problem: Intermittently, neither withSuccessHandler nor withFailureHandler ever fires. The page stays stuck on its initial "loading" state indefinitely. There is no timeout error, no failure callback — nothing.

What I've confirmed:

The server function itself runs correctly and returns valid data (verified via Executions log and by running it directly in the Apps Script editor).

The browser console shows this error, which comes from Google's own internal script, not my code: Uncaught SyntaxError: Failed to execute 'write' on 'Document': Unexpected token ')' at Xt (.../mae_html_u_user__bn.js) at No (...) at c (...) at a (...)

New finding from the Network tab: when the failure happens, the callback?nocache_id=...&token=... request to script.google.com does complete with a 200 OK status, but its response headers include:

Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="response.bin"

This looks like the actual root cause — instead of returning the callback payload as an inline script Google's bridge normally injects and executes, the server is (intermittently) sending it back with headers that tell the browser to treat it as a downloadable binary file rather than execute it as <script>. Since the browser never executes it, withSuccessHandler/withFailureHandler never fire, and the mae_html_u_user__bn.js internal script then throws while trying to process it, producing the SyntaxError above.

What I've ruled out:

My own code (tested with a fully reverted, unmodified copy — same failure)

Drive/OAuth permissions (revoked all access via myaccount.google.com/permissions and re-authorized — same failure)

What I've tried as a workaround: a client-side timeout + retry (2–3 attempts) + a window.addEventListener('error', ...) listener that detects the mae_html_u_user__bn.js SyntaxError and immediately retries the same google.script.run call. This reduces the impact but the underlying call still intermittently returns this malformed response.bin attachment response on the first (and sometimes second) attempt.

Question: Has anyone found the actual cause of Google intermittently sending the google.script.run callback response with Content-Disposition: attachment instead of executing it inline, or a reliable server-side/client-side workaround beyond retrying?

items.title: How to keep OIDC token validation entirely within a central Workspace service when the client registry lives in a separate HIS service (NestJS)?
items.human_voice:
I'm building a NestJS-based architecture with three pieces:

Workspace backend — acts as the central OIDC issuer (/oidc/token), using oidc-provider.

HIS service — a separate backend that owns hospital/client-specific data (auth credentials, scopes, appointment mapping) in its own schema.

Multiple clients — internal apps (e.g. Practice Hub) and external systems (hospitals) that need to authenticate via client_credentials grant and call protected APIs.

Constraint: all token issuance and validation must stay inside Workspace. HIS service should never issue or verify tokens itself — Workspace is the single source of truth for auth.

My planned schema (in Workspace's own DB):

sql

oidc_clients -- registered clients (internal + external)
oidc_resources -- protected APIs (aud values)
oidc_scopes -- permissions per resource
client_scope_grants -- which client can request which scope
issued_tokens -- token audit log, supports revocation
auth_attempts -- login attempt log (success/fail)

The specific problem: hospital client data (credentials, which scopes they're allowed) is naturally owned by HIS service, not Workspace — but I don't want HIS service to do any part of token issuance/validation itself. Right now I'm considering two approaches and I'm not sure which is the correct/idiomatic pattern:

Fully centralize: Workspace owns all client records (including hospitals) directly in oidc_clients, and HIS service only reads/writes hospital-specific business data (appointment mapping, hospital auth credentials) separately — with no client/scope data duplicated on the HIS side at all.

Federated validation: Workspace still signs every token, but delegates the "is this client valid, what scopes do they have" check to HIS service via an internal call (e.g. POST /internal/oidc/validate-client), since HIS service already manages hospital onboarding.

Questions:

Given the constraint that Workspace must remain the sole token issuer, is option 1 (fully centralized client registry) the more standard/correct approach, or is option 2 (federated validation, centralized signing) a legitimate and common pattern?

If going with option 2, how do I avoid tightly coupling Workspace's token endpoint to HIS service's availability (i.e., a HIS service outage blocking all hospital logins)?

Are there existing NestJS/oidc-provider patterns or libraries for this kind of "federated validation, centralized issuance" setup, or is this something typically hand-rolled?

I'm using oidc-provider (npm) inside NestJS for the Workspace issuer. Happy to share relevant code (middleware, service structure) if useful.

items.title: Error al instalar perfil MDM en iOS: “No se encontró el certificado de identidad” + llamadas vacías
items.human_voice:
Estoy buscando ayuda con un problema que tengo con la instalación de un perfil de trabajo para un dispositivo iOS. Estoy implementando un MDM propio y tengo problemas para instalar el profile en iOS.

El perfil sí se descarga y sí intenta instalarse, pero falla con el error:

“No se encontró el certificado de identidad de ‘MDM Enrollment – XXXXXXXX’”

(Este mensaje corresponde al payload com.apple.mdm).

Además, cuando el dispositivo intenta hacer el primer check-in, la petición llega a mi backend completamente vacía: sin MessageType, sin Topic, sin UDID ni ningún otro campo del body MDM.

Qué he hecho

Generé la identidad del dispositivo (PKCS#12) con openssl. Los comandos que usé fueron:

openssl genrsa -out identity.key 2048
openssl req -new -key identity.key -out identity.csr -sha256 -subj “/CN=MDM Vendor CSR/O=nombreEmpresa/C=US”
openssl x509 -inform der -in AppleWWDRCAG3.cer -out wwdr.pem
openssl x509 -inform der -in AppleIncRootCertificate.cer -out apple_root.pem
cat MDM_Certificate_From_Apple.pem wwdr.pem apple_root.pem > mdm_chain.pem

Con eso genero un PKCS#12 de identidad y lo incluyo en el perfil como payload com.apple.security.pkcs12, con su password.

Apple Push Portal

El certificado .pem emitido por Apple (MDM push certificate) se carga correctamente en el servidor MDM y se está usando para APNS.

Generación del perfil MDM

El .mobileconfig se construye con estos datos principales (resumen del XML):

<dict>
<key>PayloadType</key> com.apple.mdm
<key>ServerURL</key> https://api.midominio.com/ios/v1/command/...
<key>CheckInURL</key> https://api.midominio.com/ios/v1/checkin/...
<key>Topic</key> com.apple.mgmt.External.<token>
<key>IdentityCertificateUUID</key> <uuid-del-p12>
<key>AccessRights</key> 8191
</dict>

Además del payload com.apple.mdm, el perfil incluye:

Root CA propia (payload com.apple.security.root)
Certificado del servidor para pinning
Certificado PKCS#12 del dispositivo (com.apple.security.pkcs12)

Firma del .mobileconfig

El perfil lo firmo con openssl smime usando el certificado del MDM push:

openssl smime -sign -signer MDM_Certificate_From_Apple.pem -inkey mdm_push.key -in profile.mobileconfig -out signed.mobileconfig -outform der -nodetach

En el iPhone se ve como: “Firmado por: MDM Profile Signer — Sin verificar”, que entiendo que es normal para un root propio.

EL PROBLEMA
A) iOS no encuentra la identidad del dispositivo

Al intentar instalar el perfil aparece:

“No se encontró el certificado de identidad de ‘MDM Enrollment – XXX’”.

Pero:
- El PKCS#12 está incluido en el perfil
- La password es correcta
- La UUID del PKCS#12 coincide exactamente con IdentityCertificateUUID en el payload com.apple.mdm

B) El primer check-in llega vacío

Cuando el dispositivo hace el primer check-in, la petición llega así:

POST /ios/v1/checkin/…
Content-Type: application/x-apple-aspen-mdm-checkin
Body: (vacío)

En lugar de algo como:

{ “MessageType”: “Authenticate”, “Topic”: “…”, “UDID”: “…”, … }

Mi duda
¿El error de “no se encontró el certificado de identidad” y el body vacío del check-in pueden deberse a alguno de estos puntos?

El PKCS#12 que generé (clave, CSR o cómo lo empaqueto en el payload com.apple.security.pkcs12)
La forma en que estoy firmando el .mobileconfig con openssl smime
El chain PEM (mdm_chain.pem) que armé para APNS
Algún detalle del XML del perfil que esté mal formado y haga que iOS no llegue a cargar el certificado de identidad

Agradezco cualquier orientación. He leído la documentación oficial de Apple MDM pero no encuentro una explicación clara para este fallo.

items.title: How to handle excessive self pity
items.human_voice:
Sometimes my 11 year-old child will fall to excessive self pity. Two examples:

He was very angry about something and tossed away his phone, a corner of the phone cracked and he thought he had broken it completely and permanently. I heard him wailing from the street 200 meters away. I thought something terrible had happed, like maybe he fell and seriously injured himself. His frustration is perfectly understandable: he was already frustrated and then he lost his temper and thought he broke his favourite and most expensive play-thing. But he actively fuels the fire, the crying goes on when all the tears are spent, in a theatrical manner. He throws himself on the couch, grinds his teeth, balls his fists.

Another example: The teacher gaves us exercises to practice writing and spelling at home to help speed up his writing. He hates doing this because its school-work outside school and unlike regular homework this is not something the whole class has to do. He procastrinates, laments how unfair it is he has to do this while his friends don't, then claims he cannot spell and will do everything wrong anyway. He then cries, holds the pencil limply in his hand. While focussing on making a theater and arguing with parents he will make silly mistakes, like not finishing a word or forgetting letters, this fuels more crying and 'see I can't do this'. Last time he was hitting himself in the head with both fists after spending almost 1 hour on writing down two sentences and 5 words.

Again, this is a frustrating situation, but he is making it so much worse. The task is intended to last 15 minutes.
I understand I should avoid these situations and help him deal with frustrations but sometimes frustrating things happen. I have read 'How to talk to kids' and I try not to tell him off for his feelings, but I do want him to stop fanning the flames of negative emotions.

items.title: In positive education, what phrase follows the emotional validation?
items.human_voice:
I’m watching a course on positive parenting and secure attachment, where the instructor emphasizes the importance of "validating the child’s emotions." As an example, they mention a situation where the child wants to have ice cream for breakfast, and after denying it, our job as parents "is not to avoid their frustration, but to acknowledge it." So, what we need to do is maintain boundaries and then empathize by saying things like "I know you were really looking forward to that ice cream" or "You’re feeling a bit disappointed."

When I was a child, the conversation would have been "You can’t have ice cream for breakfast," followed by "because I said so" or "just because." Then, the older family members from my generation, like cousins who now have kids aged 8-10, would say "You can’t have ice cream for breakfast," followed by a lengthy attempt to reason with the child, "because it’s not healthy," "because you already have your cereal," etc.

My question is, exactly following the positive parenting methodology and the approach recommended by the course instructor, how does the conversation continue after the phrases that validate emotions? What exactly follows after "I know you were really looking forward to that ice cream"?

どこにテキストがあるかをあつめた内容のツリー構造の表示にて、重複されて表示される箇所をなくし、正しいツリー構造で表示したい。

環境

bashの.shにて作成中

問題

理由により、treeコマンドが使えず、ダウンロードもできないlinuxにて、

どこのフォルダにテキストファイルがあるかを探して表示し、テキストファイルに出力するbashの.shを作成しているのですが、

配列がこの状態では、

#!/bin/bash

# array1の定義（テキスト保存フォルダ）
array1=(
"save"
"save/A"
"save/A/a.txt"
"save/B"
"save/B/bb1.txt"
"save/B/bb2.txt"
"save/C"
"save/C/CC"
"save/C/CC/ccc11.txt"
"save/C/CC/ccc22.txt"
"save/dddd.txt"
"save/E"
"save/E/eeeee.txt"
"saveB"
"saveB/X"
"saveB/X/x.txt"
"txtSaveC"
"txtSaveC/Y"
"txtSaveC/Y/yy.txt"
"txtSaveC/Z"
"txtSaveC/Z/zzz1a.txt"
"txtSaveC/Z/zzz2b.txt"
"saveD"
"saveD/X"
"saveD/X/x.txt"
)

# 出力用ファイル名
output_file="output..txt"

# ディレクトリ構造を生成する関数
function generate_tree {
local prefix="$1"
local current_dir="$2"

# 現在のディレクトリ内の要素を取得
local items=()
for dir in "${array1[@]}"; do
if [[ "$dir" == "$current_dir"* ]] && [[ "$dir" != "$current_dir" ]]; then
local relative_path="${dir#$current_dir/}"
if [[ "$relative_path" != *"/"* ]]; then
items+=("$dir")
fi
fi
done

# 要素を処理
for i in "${!items[@]}"; do
local item="${items[$i]}"
local name="${item##*/}"
local is_last=$(( i == ${#items[@]} - 1 ))

# ディレクトリ

echo "$prefix└── $name" | tee -a "$output_file"
generate_tree "$prefix " "$item"
else

generate_tree "$prefix│ " "$item"
fi
else
# ファイル
if [[ $is_last -eq 1 ]]; then
echo "$prefix└── $name" | tee -a "$output_file"
else
echo "$prefix├── $name" | tee -a "$output_file"
fi
fi
done
}

# メイン処理
> "$output_file" # 出力ファイルを初期化
echo "テキスト保存フォルダ" | tee "$output_file"
generate_tree "" ""

items.title: How to troubleshoot a failing first job search out of graduate school?
items.human_voice:
Goal
My goal with this question is to have a starting point for investigating how to become gainfully employed, and how to troubleshoot current issues with gaining employment.
Many steps require monetary (e.g. career coaches) and/or time investment (further education, certification), and so I would like to get a sense for the efficacy of such solutions before investing.
Ideally answers would give general advice/resources which I could further investigate on my own to make decisions based on my circumstances, although specific suggestions based on my background (below) are also welcome.

Background
Three months ago I earned a Ph.D. in physics from a state university in a mid-sized city in the U.S.
Six months prior I had started applying to technical R&D roles, researcher/postdoc roles at the same university, and higher ed teaching positions.
These were all confined to the greater metro area, as most of my friends and my long-term romantic partner live here.
I got a handful of interviews and started networking with people who had gone to the same (small) college for undergrad as me.
The only offer that I received was an adjunct instructor position at a local small college, and I only received it because an instructor that I had been a teaching assistant for had previously worked at this college.
I ultimately declined the position because I thought at the time that I could get full-time work elsewhere.
About a month before graduating I started applying to lower level jobs: entry engineering positions, high school teaching positions, tutoring gigs, etc, none of which I received an offer from (although I did get one interview for a teaching position).
At this point I have submitted hundreds of applications over nine months, had networking conversations with tens of (friendly) people in industry, and received zero full-time offers, and only one part-time offer.

What I have tried

Networking: Most of the people that I talked to had basically fallen into their roles (i.e. been recommended by a friend or supervisor), and so I didn't get a lot of helpful advice on landing a job. Putting them down as referrals did significantly increase my chances of getting an interview at their respective companies, however.
University Career Counselor: Gave minor feedback on resumes/cover letters, suggested I network, and that I expand my job search to the whole country.
Seeking lower level positions: I've actually received a lower response rate from entry-level positions than from senior level positions, I suppose because of the Ph.D. on my resume.
Headhunter: Offered to put me in contact with a professor regarding his start-up. Unfortunately this professor is known to be emotionally abusive so I declined, and when I asked if he had any other leads he did not respond.

What I am currently doing

Trade apprenticeship: I'm currently enrolled in a 5-year apprenticeship program for a trade. Not my ideal, but it will pay the bills in the meantime.
Engineering grad school: I'm applying to 2-year programs in engineering for next fall. This would be much faster than the apprenticeship, allow me to solve more technical problems, and seem to be in line with the job postings I see (many Mechanical Engineering postings).
However I'm unsure that this would actually help me land a job, and I'm afraid hiring managers would see this as suspicious.
Geographically expanding my search: I've started to apply to jobs nation-wide. No interviews yet for jobs outside of the metro area.

Any suggestions for what to do, or how I can come to a better understanding of how job-searching works are appreciated.

items.title: リテラルの取り扱い方
items.human_voice:
Haskellの超初心者です．下記のようなプログラムを作成しました．

data Natnum = Zero | S Natnum deriving (Eq, Show)
c_1_1 :: Natnum -> Natnum
c_1_1 x1 = S Zero

その後，c_1_1 Zero と行えば S Zero と出ることは確認できます．

しかし，c_1_1 3 とすると，以下のエラーが発生します．

<interactive>:46:7: error:
• No instance for (Num Natnum) arising from the literal ‘3’
• In the first argument of ‘c_1_1’, namely ‘3’
In the expression: c_1_1 3
In an equation for ‘it’: it = c_1_1 3

Sは後者関数Zeroの後者関数を得られるものと思っているのですが，理解が間違っているのでしょうか．

私なりに理解しようとしたのですが，これはリテラル3がNatnumに無い，ということを言っていると考え，冒頭のプログラムを以下の様にしてみましたが，結果は同じでした．

data Natnum = Zero | Int | S Natnum deriving (Eq, Show)

リテラルを扱うときには何か特別なことをする必要があるのでしょうか．

どうぞよろしくお願いいたします．

追記
もともとは以下に示すサンプルプログラムを実行しようとしました．

data Natnum = Zero | S Natnum deriving (Eq, Show)

succ :: Natnum -> Natnum
succ x = S x

u_2_2 :: Natnum -> Natnum -> Natnum
u_2_2 x1 x2 = x2

add :: Natnum -> Natnum -> Natnum
add x Zero = x
add x (S y) = S (add x y)

multi :: Natnum -> Natnum -> Natnum
multi x Zero = Zero
multi x (S y) = add (multi x y) x

foo :: Natnum -> Natnum
foo x = (S . S) x

bar :: Natnum -> Natnum
bar x = multi x x

baz x y = add x y

daz x y = (foo . bar)(baz x y)

dee x y = (bar . foo)(u_2_2 x y)

このプログラムを

dee 2 3

と実行したのですが，前述の様なエラーが出ました．

このため，そもそもこのサンプルがおかしいのではと考えた次第です．

items.title: How to demonstrate leadership/Mentoring Skills

I’m not expected to review or comment on coworkers’ pull requests, even when I’m explicitly tagged as a reviewer. In my previous organization, senior engineers conducted detailed reviews, and leads provided a final high-level review. That process helped ensure alignment and mentorship, which feels absent here.

When engineers present demos or proof-of-concepts to the team, I’ve been instructed by my manager to remain silent and not offer feedback, opinions, or suggestions unless explicitly asked. I’ve followed this guidance and have stayed silent in nearly every meeting for the past six months. However, I later received feedback from my manager that I have “too much attitude” and that I only speak when called upon, which feels contradictory to the earlier direction.

I think the owner would feel like I'm jumping ship to a competitor, as they provide a similar service. I thought about asking one of our clients client. Unfortunately the client I had worked most frequently with wasn't happy with our service and recently switched providers.

Prior to my current job I had a relatively short term contract which was fully remote. I know it sounds strange but half way through the contract the manager of the team I was working on switched teams and we didn't really get a replacement. I could ask another contractor if I could use him as a reference.

The job before that one, I was laid off on good terms. There are a couple people there that I think would still give me a reference but it's been a couple years since I've worked with them. I also do volunteer work (in a completely different field) and could ask for references from the organizers. Also I'm concerned how close it is to Christmas that people might already be on vacation.

Who should I try to use as a reference? How should I ask if it's still OK to use them as a reference and how often should I do this? Should I mention that I'm asking because the prospective employer wants several references and I currently work with just one person?

items.title: Request offer details before reference check
items.human_voice:
I passed the technical interviews for a company, the only things that remain are a visit to the office and to have dinner with the founders.

I'm doubtful that this company is the right fit, even though I still need to confirm (I still need to know the salary and get a better sense for the company's culture during the visit).

That being said, so far, I wasn't requested for references.
If they asked for references before making the offer, I'd feel quite bad about wasting my referees time for something I'll unlikely accept. So:

Is it ok to inquire about details of the offer if they ask for references? If so, how would you phrase the request?

items.title: Is ritualized confession a sign of a bad culture of failure?
items.human_voice:
I’m part of a team that, in my view, has a somewhat unusual approach to failure. Whenever something goes wrong, the person responsible openly admits the mistake and apologizes. There’s no blaming, and no apparent fear of sanctions. The team members have been working together for several years, while I’m relatively new, so I’m still trying to understand the dynamics.

To be clear, I generally see this as a sign of psychological safety. Being able to admit mistakes in a blameless way is healthy, and errors are a very human part of work. That said, I don’t think every mistake needs to be explicitly highlighted each time—unless there’s something to learn from it, or someone genuinely wants to take responsibility and reflect openly.

What bothers me slightly is the almost “ritualized” nature of these confessions. It feels like an expectation rather than a spontaneous act, and I worry it subtly shifts the focus from fixing the issue to focusing on the individual.

So I’m wondering: am I overthinking this and seeing a problem where there isn’t one, or could this pattern be masking a deeper cultural issue within the team?

items.title: How should I handle uneven project visibility and recognition within a team of project managers?
items.human_voice:
I’m a project manager in a team of PMs plus one team lead. Everyone has their own projects and several of us are new to the team. We were all hired as project managers, have roughly comparable professional experience and receive the same compensation; none of us are beginners or junior PMs.

Something uncomfortable has caught my attention, and I’m unsure how to handle it in a professional and constructive way.

I have been assigned projects that are more internal, enabling and long-term in nature and that also include providing support to other team members in refining their work when required.

My question is about the best professional approach going forward:
Would it be appropriate for me to briefly report on my own progress and results in the next team meeting, even if my manager does not explicitly invite me to do so?

More generally, how should one handle situations where project visibility and public recognition are uneven within a team, despite similar roles, experience, and compensation?

I’m looking for advice on how to navigate this constructively and professionally

items.title: How should I communicate effiently a possible GDPR violation regarding an implementation upon codebase?
items.human_voice:
On the company I work as a full employee (not contractor), I had implemented a mechanism that stores scanned identification files documents. For it I took consideration the sensitivity of these types of documents and used a secure mechanism for it.

However, my team leader instructed me to implement a less secure mechanism due to issues with front-end team. I considered this a violation of GDPR, therefore I escalated the issue to my Team Leader's manager and got notified.

I also asked for time to implement a secure mechanism. He told me to issue a ticket for it, so I did, and notified my team leader regarding this.

But I am afraid that if a breach happens I would need to run to patch it up upon rush and I want to avoid that, because I would gain nothing. So I though this approach in order to communicate the impact of this:

I would wait until less secure piece of code to be deployed, then after 2 week notice period I would send an email to the Supervisor's Manager and CC the company founders as well.

The email would say the following:

There is a weak mechanism that would cause financial damage upon the company, indicating the penalties that GDPR mentions upon improper implementation.

I would ask this task to be prioritized.

If no security measures would be implemented upon a data breach would also mean my immediate resignation.

If no security measures taken in 2 month period, I would report this upon Data Protection Agency.

But is this the professional way to deal with this?

My goal is to force the company take notice about this, give me time to implement security mechanism, before it is too late.

items.title: Lead rudely demands fixing alleged error on weekend
items.human_voice:
I'm a developer in a software development company. I work here for about a year and a half.

Today, Sunday, is an important deployment of our product. They chose almost the latest version which wasn't tested that much (27 November). Perhaps, there were some crucial features whose delivery couldn't, in their view, be postponed.

About an hour ago, our lead posted in our work chat. He included some code snippet, tagged me, and complained about some error that, in his view, was caused by my changes. I haven't investigated it yet. The related task was indeed done by me some weeks ago. It was tested, accepted by the QA, and closed.

Friday, the lead wrote an email to the project's developers asking to be in touch in case something happens. However, I never agreed to work this weekend. It is neither part of my legal obligations as an employee, nor par for the course in our job as an informal practice (at least, not in our department).

This approach was different from what the lead did in October in a similar situation. Back then, he explicitly asked for someone to be on-duty Sunday. I was the only one who volunteered and came to the office as usual. Nothing bad happened, but I got my overtime pay as promised. My speculation is the lead hoped we were going to be lucky again, but to have everyone at his disposal in case we weren't – while taking no unconditional compensation obligations (if nothing happens, no-one gets paid – an on-duty developer would be paid regardless, on the other hand).

I heard that overwork, working weekends is part of the American work culture. It is not, however, part of the European work culture. I reside in Russia that has yet to fully embrace European values, yet it is not really part of work culture here as well.

The job market is tough today, especially for a developer under 3-5 years of experience like me. I don't think it is realistic to expect a new job offer, especially this time of year. It would be a heavy blow, if I lose the job. That said, it is also important to maintain boundaries and adhere to professional standards.

How do I act in this situation in a professional manner?

UPD: It turned out there was invalid data in the DB. It was not a conclusion of mine — it was determined by an independent party that I had no influence over whatsoever (the head of another department responsible for that particular functionality). Graceful handling of that invalid data was never part of any task that I'm aware of. The task was tested on valid DB data.

items.title: Soft drinks in my office’s community fridge keeps disappearing. How to deal with this?
items.human_voice:
We have a community fridge at my new workplace where people normally leave their lunch.

As I enjoy soft drinks, I thought I would treat myself to leaving a bottle of soft drink to take a glass every now and then. I wouldn't mind if someone occasionally took a glass from it.

I have just started at this new place, so navigating office dynamics is a bit delicate. Most people haven't got to know me beyond official introductions.

Yet, my bottle has consistently disappeared. People are consuming it way more than I am willing to tolerate. No one has ever asked me before taking a cup (though I didn't write my name on it, so the person wouldn't even know whom to ask). The fridge has always had a sign claiming "the fridge is shared, its content are not. Do not consume what is not yours".

I am not sure how to proceed. I wouldn't like to issue a complaint leading to the first thing many people would remember me by would be this complaint. I've considered labelling the bottle with my name, marking the level, or wrapping it on a plastic bag. Using single-serving cans instead of a 2L bottle would make the cost meaningfully higher. Pretty sure this is a well known and studied problem, but I am not satisfied with the ideas I've got from AI.

Update: Nobody brings any drinks nor water to the fridge. All users seem to just leave a packed meal. I had never seen a bottle on the fridge other than mine (though the sample is small so far).

Update 2: I haven't written my name because I also didn't want to bring attention to the fact I bringing soft drinks for myself. If the rule on the fridge is "don't take what not yours", and there are never any other bottles of any kind on the fridge, there was no room for honest mistakes. My name should have been unnecessary.

I am checking and digesting answers before deciding how to proceed. In the meantime, I'm just keeping a bottle on my desk and filling a glass full of ice when I feel like it. It's quite suboptimal but does the trick for now.

Nonetheless, I've discovered there is an ongoing event with lots of external people on the floor below, some of these people have been using our kitchen, so maybe the thieves are temporary visitors that will soon be gone. There is no point on taking any action before this event is finished and those visitors are gone.

Can anyone who uses employee monitoring software verify this info?

items.title: Is my manager being reasonable or is this discrimination? New grad, autism diagnosis, probation at risk. (UK based)
items.human_voice:
I’m a new grad who recently started my first professional job. My manager told me she was considering failing my probation and removing me from the role. After that conversation, I disclosed that I’m autistic (diagnosed). The probation meeting was then paused, and my performance has since improved.

We had a meeting with Genius Within (an occupational health org that advises on reasonable adjustments). HR and my manager joined.

Here’s what confused me:

My manager told them my performance had improved — but then listed “behaviour problems” she claims show I’m not engaged:

I don’t make eye contact with her

She saw me wearing my coat and holding my bag in an internal meeting (it was the last meeting of the day)

She saw me eating during a meeting

She saw me occasionally scrolling my phone during an 8-hour team away-day seminar

None of these were flagged to me at the time. She’s using them as examples of me “not paying attention,” even though HR said individually these behaviours aren’t normally concerning.

Given that I’m autistic and these are all common autistic traits or coping behaviours, is this reasonable management? Or does it sound like she’s pathologising normal ND behaviours despite my improved performance?

I’m trying to figure out if this is fair criticism or if I’m being judged on stuff that shouldn’t matter. What would you make of this?

Even HR agreed with me that no eye contact could mean I am just autistic, not that I am not paying attention and that I engaged with the reasonable adjustments process quite closely thus far so I am obviously engaged. However, HR also told me that those may be signs I am not a good cultural fit for the company, although he did tell me that when he first turned up, he was in a 3 piece suit every day for the first few weeks.

items.title: Should I mention a failed/unsuccessful entrepreneurship on my resume to account for a 2 year career gap? If so, what are some best practices?
items.human_voice:
Context:
I’m returning to the job market after a two-year gap and want to present this period accurately on my resume.

My last full-time role in my domain (embedded software development and technical program management in DoD and medical device sectors) ended in summer 2023.
I spent the next year actively job hunting — many interviews, but no offers.
In mid-2024, I pivoted to building a business focused on small business automation using AI. I worked on it for 6–12 months, but due to personal health and family issues, I had to pause the venture.
The business didn’t generate revenue or clients, but I gained experience in automation tools, AI workflows, and small business operations

Question:
Given that the business didn’t produce external results (e.g., revenue, clients), how should I list it on my resume to account for the 2023–2025 gap?

Is it appropriate to include it as a formal role (e.g., Founder)?
Should I omit it entirely?
Are there accepted formats or phrasing that frame this constructively?

I’m looking for resume formatting guidance or examples that align with professional standards.

Why this question is different from Irrelevant jobs vs long employment gap:

This question is specific to being an entrepreneur and never receiving revenue
If you never had revenue, then myself and others might think that they might as well have been unemployed since they do not have anything to show for it
While "irrelevant jobs" still means you were at least employed, even if the job is not necessarily related to your field, you still have something to show. You are still able to show that you were working somewhere.

items.title: Is it illegal for the employee to work off the clock, of their own volition, without being asked?
items.human_voice:
Is it illegal for the employee to work off the clock, of their own volition, without being asked?

I worked in a position where, to accomplish every duty assigned but with a limit of 40 hours, I had to choose whether to work home/punch-out then remain on site (working off the clock), or miss deadlines.

I am under the impression that it is illegal for my employer to ask me to do that, but not illegal if I volunteer to do it of my own volition.

Is that correct? Or was I breaking a law or causing them to?

Location: Colorado, United States

(N.B. I did write up a doc totaling the meetings and reports and other commitments and explained to my supervisor that there was simply not enough time to do all the other things. They did not respond directly, but a few weeks later, I was then asked to resign and the primary reason given was time management.).

For clarification after choosing a best answer, this was a non-exempt (hourly) position in a non-profit organization.

items.title: Asked for help without enough information
items.human_voice:
I am a software developer. I have worked on a component which a colleague has deployed and is supporting the customer. He has verbally suggested there may be a bug in a feature I have worked on describing the situation and asked me to think about it. Because his description was quick and contained several points and the feature was years ago and I barely remembered it, I asked him to provide an email containing details and offered to help double-check the code.

After I read the email, it became clear that he hadn't done his responsibility in proving whether the problem was a bug in my feature or his deployment setup. He had also passed it off as a quick task that I could do, but the problem stated in the email clearly was more complex and involved. It also occurred to me that the feature was tested and released, so checking the code shouldn't show anything new.

What is a good option to take? Should I ask him to prove the bug is in my feature? Should I ask for clarification on my responsibility? Whether he wants help to debug his deployment setup or just wants me to double-check the code.

items.title: Should the company require employee pictures on the company directory?
items.human_voice:
My company has a corporate directory that has a picture for each entry. As with my MS Teams account, I set my picture to the photo that is on my badge but several of my colleagues have pictures of their pets or a landscape or whatever.

The problem, it is a big company with lots of people all over the US. Most of the people I work with, I have never met in person. We talk every few days over MS Teams but almost never with videochat because we have work documents to discuss.

When I talk to a people, it is good to have at least some idea what they look like, if for nothing other than to know if they are 22 or 72, or somewhere in between.

Am I being unreasonable asking that their directory or MS Teams picture be of them, not something they find amusing? They can “have fun” with their picture on Facebook (or stackexchange) but for the company, being a grouch, I would like to ask that we have a picture of them.

Update, maybe a better question would be, "Is it unprofessional" to have a picture of other than the person?

items.title: If asked in an interview, how do you phrase you like a hands off management style?
items.human_voice:
I had an interview. Afterward I was given the feedback I came across a bit antisocial.

I think the biggest disconnect was when the interviewer asked me what kind of management style I prefer.

In my experience, I work well when I'm told what the goal is and left to achieve it. I work well with scheduled check ins, for example weekly meetings. My productivity goes down when being micromanaged or I feel like someone is standing behind me waiting for me to make a mistake for them to point out.

How should I phrase this in an interview?

Sometimes I'm bad at phrasing these types of things without coming across of anti-social. I realize unscheduled interruptions are sometimes inevitable, but I still appreciate an effort to schedule meetings as I find I'm more productive that way.

For context this was a tech position and the interviewer was talking about how some people liked to "keep their head down while doing work".

items.title: What's a good way to ask for work when you completed your task without sounding repetitive and pushy
items.human_voice:
Context:

I’m a vendor working on a client project where tasks are assigned by my American client manager, either through email or an internal project management tool. I’m required to log my working hours in an Excel sheet so my actual manager can review and present them for client approval during monthly meetings. Although I sometimes work 10–11 hours a day, I usually log around 8 hours to maintain consistency and meet the weekly 40-hour requirement. Sometimes I readjust work hours per day to just show 40 hours even if I work more as my organization bills the client for this time.

Issue I face:

At times, I complete all my assigned tasks before my shift ends, leaving me with extra time. When this happens, I usually message my client manager on Slack saying, “I’m done with my tasks for the day. Please let me know if I can work on something else.” However, I worry that sending this message frequently—sometimes daily—might come across as repetitive, pushy, or inconsiderate of his busy schedule, especially given the cultural differences and his workload. He’s always polite and supportive, but I’m unsure how to communicate above without coming across as repetitive or pushy.

items.title: Is it reasonable that an assessment takes 3 weeks for a senior position?
items.human_voice:
I applied for a senior role. The company asks me to do an assessment.

They then sent me the assignment like this:

As promised, I'm sending you our assessment here. I've attached the assessment to this email. Good luck, and once you've completed the assessment, I'd love to receive your results by email!

By looking at the requirements, I said this assessment will take approximately 3 weeks, they said OK.

I understand the company's point of view. It's a 'show me what you got' mentality. On the flip side, I believe it's also a lack of trust to the job applicant.

What is the maximum amount of time an employer may ask for in an assessment?

Is a 3 weeks assessment a red flag?

The whole point about it, is that I already did the 3 weeks assessment. I made something which is really state-of-the-art. But now, it left me with a bad feeling. I should be happy about it, but I'm not.

I seriously want to write them a rejection because of the possibility for the free work exploit. What would you do?
