items.title: How do I make the best of a busy resume?
items.human_voice:
I'm looking for jobs in one of two fields: technical writing, and Excel/VBA development. My work history has many examples of both, mostly short-term contract or freelance jobs.

I want to customize a resume for each job I apply to. The problem is:

If I list all of the jobs for the last 10 years, half of them would not be relevant to the position I'm applying for.
If I list only the jobs relevant to the position, the resume will show a lot of gaps of 6-12 months. (Gaps between jobs are normal, especially if you leave out "survival" jobs. But in my case they'd include substantial jobs in the other career.)
Because there were so many short-term jobs over the last 10 years, the resume goes on well over 2 pages, even if I'm omitting the irrelevant ones.

How to handle such issues?

Should I label the "Experience" section "Relevant Experience" instead?
Should I have an "entry" for each gap that says something like "working in a different career"?
Do I stop at 2 pages, regardless of the number of years it goes back?
Anything else I can do?

items.title: What my boss really wanted to say
items.human_voice:
I recently had a conversation with my boss, and he said:

“Since you’re open to work, we won’t be holding you.”

I’m unsure how to interpret this.

For context:

I work in a stable company (no layoffs).

My LinkedIn profile shows “open to work.”

My last performance review was very good.

I haven’t been told I’m being let go.

Does this phrase generally mean that my boss is considering terminating my employment, or just that the company won’t try to stop me if I decide to leave?

I’d like to understand what such a statement usually implies in a professional context so I can prepare appropriately.

items.title: CEO told staff to just leave if we have concerns and trust issues with leadership - what now?
items.human_voice:
I work for a small UK company and have done for 4 years. There's been a lot of upheaval recently, restructuring, 3 rounds of redundancies in just over 2 years, and very mixed messaging from leadership about the company's direction. It's created a lot of insecurity and confusion across the business.

I (and others) have raised concerns multiple times about the breakdown of trust between leadership and staff, and about how the communication around these changes is handled. These concerns aren't about the redundancies themselves, as I understand some things are inevitable, but about the way things are framed and communicated. The pattern at the moment is promises of growth and opportunity one week, followed by talks of cost-cutting and redundancies being announced the next. It's been emotionally exhausting and demoralising for the whole team.

During an all-company meeting this week, I asked (anonymously) how leadership planned to address the breakdown of trust between them and employees. The CEO's exact words in response were:

I'm afraid if … there is a breakdown of trust, there is no way I can rebuild it and I would ask you openly to please volunteer yourself to leave the business

This has really shaken people. It felt dismissive and almost like an ultimatum, as though if we have concerns, we’re not welcome. I was planning to handle my concerns informally through HR, but after that comment, I've decided to treat it as a formal grievance.

Firstly, am I doing the right thing? For context I am currently on maternity leave so I can't just go and get another job. I also genuinely love my job, care about the company mission and the people I work with.

Secondly, would a comment like this from the CEO, in the context of all of the existing upheaval, mixed messaging and distrust amount to a breach of the implied term of mutual trust and confidence? Could this (alongside a pattern of poor communication and uncertainty) form part of a constructive dismissal claim if things continue? And practically, should I be contacting ACAS at this stage, or wait to see how HR handle the grievance first?

I'm not trying to cause trouble. I genuinely care about my work and my team, and want to find a way forward that improves trust and communication. But this feels like the company is pushing employees out emotionally before anything official happens.

Any advice from those familiar with employment law or HR best practice would be really appreciated.

items.title: Must I read a data privacy notice included in a job application?
items.human_voice: I'm attempting to apply for a job with a major US company. The job application requires an assessment performed by a third party. In this assessment is a (in my opinion very long and legal) Data Privacy Notice, which I must confirm I have read and understood. I do not want to read it. Even if I read it, I will probably feel dishonest claiming I have read and understood it. Yet I have just "certif[ied] that all of the information I have provided on this application and in the hiring process is correct and complete." I do not want to lie. Feeling that I have done so will jeopardize this whole endeavor for me, as I will feel that I have gotten the job under false pretenses. I know no one can really answer this for me, but I'm curious as to others' thoughts on this moral dilemma. Do employers really expect people to read all this? Am I a liar if I blow through it like I would in other cases of less importance (downloading an app, for example)?

items.title: Interview help - How to deal with allegations of misconduct in a previous role?
items.human_voice:
I've been selected to an interview for a part-time teaching assistant job for smart and gifted children. The role is to assist instructors in teaching, maintain class order, monitor students' progress and explaining questions to students.

I had a conflict from a previous educational internship that may come up, if they ask about the summer internships I did last summer. The owner claimed my attendance record was inconsistent with my real attendance, that I had "interpersonal challenges" and that I was "reported" for "inappropriate language." I was not shown these claims until my termination. The owner did not attach any evidence to support her claims. I have complained to my internship scheme and the company owner and my supervisor are currently under investigation. I wish to ensure I can address this appropriately while focusing on my other mentoring experiences.

My supervisor is under investigation for bullying and the owner is under investigation for unprofessional behavior. Both things that undermine the employment relationship.

There were other issues such as being mandated to report minor things as a "safeguarding" issue, for instance minorly overmature talk, eating too much junk food. At the same time the instructions were sometimes vague and illogical- the time management techniques I gave in my course design were thought of as "competition tactics" and my supervisor wanted me to put a table of appropriate versus inappropriate behavior, when the DSM-5-TR criteria for mental disorders would be more standardized than the teachers' subjective opinions.

How should I address this educational internship that ended in my termination? Do I leave it and simply say I was a part-time undergraduate researcher in my university (which is true)?

items.title: How to find the right team fit?
items.human_voice:
I’m a software professional currently facing challenges with a TechLead that are affecting my productivity and confidence. I want to handle the situation constructively and explore options for improving my work environment.

Here’s the general situation:
I work carefully to ensure quality, which sometimes slows down my pace.
Some tasks have been complex with unclear priorities, and I’ve spent extra time understanding them before delivering.
My TechLead has been very critical and direct, sometimes minimizing contributions, and has mentioned that my style is different.
I feel I need some autonomy to approach tasks step-by-step, while still having clear priorities upfront.
I also feel like there’s no room to make mistakes, which makes it stressful to ask questions or try new approaches.

I’m concerned about:
How to communicate this to my manager in a professional way that highlights the impact on my work without blaming the TechLead.
Whether I should request a team transfer or try to improve collaboration in the current team.
How to identify a team or leader that fits my working style and allows me to be effective.

Questions:
How can I frame my concerns about a micromanaging TechLead in a way that is neutral, professional, and focused on work outcomes?
What strategies can I use in a meeting with my manager to discuss these challenges and explore options, including a possible team transfer?
How can I evaluate whether a team or leader is a good fit for my working style and learning approach before joining a new team?
Any advice or examples of how others have handled similar situations would be greatly appreciated.

items.title: Repeated unjustified comments "your demonstration sucks" during a presentation
items.human_voice:
During the presentation of my invention to our director (n+3 above me), I explained how it helps in drone navigation, and I showed actual demonstration flight paths and data.
The n+3 works in a totally unrelated field, but he knows how my invention is used and my co-inventor and I have showed him how useful it is.

The n+3 seemed to have misunderstood the purpose of our patent, and repeated several times over the course of the Q&A section of my presentation "your demonstration sucks".

While my colleague literally shouted to the director that we had already provided multiple clear demonstrations, I calmly asked the n+3 to explain what he expects to see (he replied vaguely and not to the point, we had clear material to show the difference with/without the invention). We also answered all his questions. I told him that his comment was not very respectful for our work. He insisted and repeated his comment, but still without any explanation about it.

I am open to constructive comments about my work, any aspect of my work, and I have faced harsh criticisms before (while in another division of the same institute), but I have never heard such an unjustified comment from someone who doesn't have any competence in the field where I am working.

Such a comment depends on the culture of the workplace, that and the personality of the supervisor.
I would have accepted it if it had been accompanied by reasonable and/or professional, technical explanations and justifications. But it appeared like a free criticism.

I reported the n+3's comments and attitude to HR, but no action were taken.

How should I follow up on this? More generally, how can I deal with this kind of comments when they are not accompanied by explanations?

Some background, including technical.

I am a researcher in a non-profit R&D institute in Taiwan.
I work on drones, specifically drone navigation (Visual Inertial Odometry (VIO), to be precise).
VIO requires one to characterize (measure) the noise of Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs),
the traditional approach for this is to acquire IMU data during several hours, perform a specific well-known analysis (Allan variance (AVAR) analysis) and then multiply the obtained figures by what we like to call "magic numbers". They are multiplicative factors that accounts for the difference between and dynamic (in-flight) noises.
My invention is to avoid the use of magic numbers and obtain an accurate dynamic/in-flight noise.
At the end of my presentation, before the Q&A, the n+3 made this comment "I don't really believe in magic numbers". It was surprising, since my presentation started with the cons of using magic numbers; so I naturally replied "we don't either and this is why we have this patent".
IMU noise characterization is a very important and well-known part of VIO, but no methods is similar to ours
he refused our patent on the grounds that he thought that a potential customer of ours would not buy it.
I am considering open sourcing my approach

Edit: addressing some comments, more details

n+3: I am at level n, the director is n+3 (3rd level above me)
"you demonstration sucks". I should have provided more explanations: the n+3's comment wasn't about my presentation skills (oral or written) but about the proofs of the advantages and usefulness of our invention. He didn't ask a question when he made that comment, but we did in return, to inquire what he wanted to see, and what was to be improved. It was our job to explain, we did, in many possible ways. At some point we were confused: the n+3 seemed to reject our evidences without being able to clearly state what was missing or unclear. Part of the demos showed a drone drifting away (without the invention) vs a drone flying according to the planned path (with the invention), and this, without having to use "magic numbers" (obtained by trial and error, these numbers are per-drone hardware parameters), and this without having to spend hours of data acquisition every time. We felt (my colleague and I) that it appeared as if the n+3 was refusing simple, evidence based, reality based facts: no more drift with the invention; and he couldn't explain what was not convincing about it.
the n+3 has a PhD in an unrelated field, he had challenged the usefulness of VIO for a long time (VIO allows a drone to fly without a GPS under certain conditions)
the n+2 supported us but couldn't decide (she had just arrived in our institute)
the n+1 is an engineer, newly appointed to that management level by the n+3, some colleagues says he is sold to whatever the n+3 says
The audience: engineers, sales, and marketing.
The presentation itself:

it was peer-reviewed and I have practiced it
it was the third time I present the topic
it was conducted in English, Q&A in Mandarin, there was no language barrier.
When I have an important presentation such as this one, I explain to my wife (not a technical person) what I will be talking about to make sure the concept can be understood by people not "skilled in the art"

Patent specific presentations: internal guidelines, which i have followed, requires one to address the prior arts, technical principles and advantages, whether or not it can easily be infringed, and the potential customers.
I'm the only foreigner in the department, my colleagues are all Taiwanese.
the comment (repeated 7 times throughout the Q&A session): I perceived it as disrespectful, highly dismissive of our work but above all lacking any scientific and constructive content.
patent application follow-up: we gave up as we felt motivations to refuse it appeared arbitrary (leaving no room for any discussion), some were unclear, lacked forward-thinking and were potentially biased. Not worth fighting for anymore.

items.title: Advice on handling communication
items.human_voice:
I am facing a situation at work and would appreciate advice on how to handle it professionally.

I completed a task that required coordination for a production deployment and communicated with the responsible team member about the delivery date. I also notified the team via the official channel that the deployment was ready. Later, I was not available to execute the deployment myself, so I sent a private message to the project manager to remind them to inform the appropriate parties.

After some time, the PM informed me that the deployment was postponed and advised me to avoid using that private communication channel.

I believe my actions were reasonable and professional, but I am concerned about being blamed. I want to maintain clear boundaries and ensure my work and communications are properly documented.

My questions:

What is the best way to handle communication with this PM?

Should private messages ever be used for urgent work-related topics, even in small teams?

items.title: How to handle a situation where I may be assessed by someone without knowledge of my work?
items.human_voice:
Now that my first 3 months are up, my manager has scheduled our first official feedback meeting. He mentioned that he plans to ask his manager (“the big boss”) for input because he thinks the big boss might have a better impression of me.

The problem is: the big boss barely knows me.
Still, I’m wondering: should I clarify in the feedback meeting that the big boss barely knows me? Or would that come across as defensive or awkward?

items.title: How can I get fired less?
items.human_voice:
I am quite new to the workforce. I am finishing a Pharmacy degree.

I have been fired 4 times from community pharmacies.

I worked 1 week cause I lied about having a car and they needed deliveries
I lied about being in 1st year pharmacy when I wasn't yet and just about to get into university.
I didn't attend my part time shifts and kept calling in sick because I was working at another pharmacy, and was too tired to go to both.
I got fired at a hospital on the 1st day because I got in a bit of a fight with the security guard and names were called cause the guard didn't think i was a worker there.

I have kept 2 jobs so far.

In my 2nd year of pharmacy I worked 1 day a week and kept that job for a year before I resigned although I did get some customer complaints that I was rude.
I kept a teaching job every week working 3 hours

I started my internship community this year and got fired after 5 months. Some of the comments I got from the manager were

you were being rude and standoffish to customers mainly communication; but customers are really rude in retail
not getting along with coworkers; I felt like a colleague was picking on me and ended up yelling at the colleague in front of the customer

At this point after finishing my degree I feel hopeless and devastated not knowing whether I can start/continue my career at this point. My end goal is to get into hospital.

I do admit I have poor work ethic, but the manager didn't mention this at the meeting, only the customer complaints and the poor relationship with my colleague.

I don't want to change careers. I have worked hard in university and have no choice but to do this career.

How can I do better and not be fired as often?

items.title: Notice/Vacation Overlap
items.human_voice:
Received a verbal offer for a new job with the expectation that the written offer will arrive early next week (I live in the US and specifically in MA). The challenge I am facing is that I have a 2 week vacation scheduled to start on the following Thursday, which would at best give me a week to 1.5 weeks worth of notice to give to my current employer.

Would it be a concern to take a less than 2 week notice period (as my new job 'prefers' that I would start before EOM)?

items.title: I have a lot of PTO to take, which will make the deadline impossible
items.human_voice:
I work as a consultant for a client fulltime. This client does not know my PTO budget. My current PTO budget has barely been used so I have a lot of days that I have to take by the end of 2025 or I lose the leave. It was not communicated to the client either. I'm assigned to a project with a very ambitious deadline that cannot be moved. This is the end of this year, the same day that all my PTO has to be taken.

The client needs my profile for future projects and it is expected that I continue there to give support on the product and to develop other products. The client (same manager) and I have agreed to work together for at least a year.

How can I best communicate that I have a lot of remaining PTOs that I have to take? How can I word it so the professional relationship between us will remain pleasant? And how can I hint that the deadline is even less feasible than expected

items.title: Why are my job applications being rejected for the past year?
items.human_voice: I have been applying to various software and IT-related jobs for the past year, but I keep getting rejections or no responses. I have updated my resume and LinkedIn profile multiple times, and I have experience in Python, SQL, web development, and cloud technologies like AWS and Azure. I am unsure whether the problem is with my resume, application approach, interview skills, or something else. I want to understand what might be causing the consistent rejections and how I can improve my chances of getting selected.

items.title: Is it wise to limit training others while serving notice, especially when the knowledge wasn't gained at current company?
items.human_voice:
I'm currently serving my notice period (11+ years experience in my field), and my manager has asked me to train a junior new joiner (with just 1 year of experience) on certain concepts that are very rarely used in this company.

Here's the catch:

These specific concepts weren't something I learnt or picked up while working here — I brought this knowledge with me from a previous job.

I'm currently under very tight deadlines, working on critical submissions that need my full attention.

Despite this, my manager is pushing me to train this junior — but strangely, hasn't asked other team members (who are far less busy) to assist with any training at all.

I strongly suspect this is more about creating the narrative that I’m easily replaceable than it is about knowledge transfer.

So I’m wondering:

Is it reasonable (or wise) to push back and not train this junior on things that weren’t even learned in this company?

If questioned, is it fair to say: “This knowledge wasn’t something I gained here, and I don’t feel comfortable training others on external knowledge that I brought in”?

Has anyone else been in a similar situation where a toxic or cunning manager tried to milk every last drop out of you during notice to make you seem dispensable?

To be clear, I’m not against helping others or doing handovers — but this feels like exploitation masked as "transition planning." Especially when others are twiddling their thumbs, and I'm being overloaded.

Curious to hear your thoughts. I work in India

items.title: New in my job, made a mistake with crediting a colleague – how should I handle this?
items.human_voice:
I’m new in my job. Recently my boss asked me to create a tool for a recurring process. The goal was to map out the workflow, relevant aspects, lessons learned, etc., so it could later be published internally as a template for future projects.

I did about 90% of the work myself, using existing documentation that had been built up over the years (mostly by people who don’t even work here anymore). Since I don’t have an IT background, I asked a colleague to review it. I expected him to take some time and look at it carefully, but instead he dropped by spontaneously and gave me some quick feedback in about 20 minutes. Some points were useful, but overall his contribution was pretty limited compared to the work I had already done.

During that conversation, I even said something like, “I’ll let the boss know we did this together.” But when I later sent the final result to my boss, I didn’t mention him by name anymore, because in my mind his contribution felt minor and rushed compared to the whole project.

Now I’ve found out that he complained to my boss and even gossiped about me, saying I didn’t acknowledge his input. He seems really upset.

I honestly feel bad, because it was never my intention to take credit for his work. Where I come from, small reviews or occasional help are often seen as “give and take” among colleagues – sometimes you mention it, sometimes you don’t. But now I’m worried I’ve made a bad impression as the “new person who exploits colleagues.”

Did I mess up badly here? How should I handle this with my colleague and with my boss going forward?

items.title: Serving Notice period but no KT happening
items.human_voice:
I'm currently working in an MNC in India, serving my 3-month notice period. Only 3 weeks remain in my notice period to complete, but they haven't found a replacement yet. KT sessions haven't started, and I was informed by my manager(who will be responsible for giving the relieving letter) that they are not able to find my replacement yet. The project is currently in the UAT testing phase and is going live just one day before my last working day. This being my first corporate job, I would like to know :

Is it normal in MNCs to not find a replacement till the end? Ideally, according to your experience, how many days before your replacement was introduced in the team?
Do they have the authority to extend my notice period even when I serve the complete 3 months of it? I heard from my people lead that until the project officially declares that you have completed all the tasks assigned, given the proper KT, they won't be releasing you. But if they are not finding a replacement in 3 MONTH LONG time period, what can I do? How come this is my responsibility to give KT when they are still giving me new tasks?
If they eventually end up asking/threatening me with a relieving letter delay, considering I don't wish to stay even one more day here, what are my rights? How to respond to such situations without burning bridges?
I read on this platform that it's better to email your manager and HR regarding knowledge transfer. What exactly should I mail? And I have 2 different HR's: exit HR and the one assigned to me since day 1, but we never connected, so who should be tagged in the mail?

would appreciate raw, honest advice. thankyou!

items.title: How to respond to interview question regarding why you left your last job without finding a new one?
items.human_voice:
I left my job two months ago. Why? Because of the following reasons:

The work was menial.
The pay was horrible.
The blame was most. We were the frontliners in the IT war without much power in our hands.
I wanted to prepare for government computer engineer job.
I could not see myself in that role for long.

Few follow up questions that interviewers can ask are:

Why could not you seek a different job instead while having your existing job?
Why could not you seek a different department in your previous company itself?

I was preparing for government job since I left my job.

Nepal has now collapsed. I do not expect any upcoming vacancies(for government computer engineer) for the near time being. At least for 1.5 years.

Now, I need to get back into industry after few months. Thus I need to be prepared to answer these questions. The most plausible one seems like "I was preparing for government computer engineer job examination and the government collapsed" (which is the reality as well). I am here to seek insights on what troubles this answer could bring and suggested ways to overcome them?

items.title: Stock disappeared from Google Finance
items.human_voice:
I'm new to trading and I had my Bayer stock BAYN with ticker DE000BAY0017 added to my Google Finance portfolio and it always used to say BAYN ETR. And now it has disappeared from my watchlist and I can no longer find it when I enter the ticker. It does show BAYN VIE but this stock price differs from what my bank says the stock is worth in my portfolio. So it must be a different stock.

Does anybody know why Google Finance does not show the exact tickers anymore?

It used to work just fine until a week ago.

Thanks in advance for any help.

I'll add some more info to my question to show that I'm not attention whoring.

The image below displays the overview on the Google Finance app. BAYN ETR is not there.

The image below shows the TradingView app which I've just installed and it does show the exact stock. The BAYN - XETR. Right at the top. Which is the one I'm looking for on Google Finance.

items.title: Does taking lots of notes look bad in an interview? Got feedback that I seemed uninterested
items.human_voice:
A recruiter contacted me about a job. The job description was short and he said he didn't have much information about the work itself. I had the interview. It was virtual and was with the manager of the team. I thought it went decently. But I got the feedback that they found me uninterested with the work and the company, and that I was hard to build rapport with. While I want to make a positive change in what I'm doing, I sometimes find it can be difficult when given not very specific feedback.

One thing I was wondering about was if I didn't spend enough time looking into the camera. I took a lot of notes, especially since I hadn't been given many details about the job in the first place. Also the interviewer talked quite a bit and talked fast (like quickly listed off 3 products that their teams uses). I sincerely was interested in the job and even said so at the end of the interview. I also asked questions about the tech stack and the team dynamics, so I'm a bit curious about how I seemed uninterested.

Should I say any of this to the recruiter or just thank him for his time?

items.title: A week of vacation and I have forgot everything I did
items.human_voice:
Looks I can not continue it, because honestly, I can not remember a bit of what I did.

Everything happened verbally recently in the last months (already unprofessional, but that is it). I remember that I had maybe multiple tasks, but I can not revive their details.

WTF? Should I visit a psychologist or politely ask my coworkers?

Remark from the future: after some days of investigation and polite talk, I slowly remembered everything. Looks I need a job where my employer has better tasks as the loud advocation of everything I hate.

items.title: Interview - Former manager messing up interview
items.human_voice:
Original Situation:

After graduating, I’ve held two jobs so far. In both roles, I consistently performed at a high level and received positive feedback throughout. Recently, I interviewed for a new opportunity, and it went well. As part of the process, the company requested two professional references.

I contacted two former managers—one from each of my previous jobs—who had both given me positive feedback in the past. In fact, one of them had already provided a successful reference that helped me land my second job. When I asked if they could provide strong references again, both agreed.

After I submitted their contact information, the company sent them reference forms. Soon after the forms were submitted, I was invited to a follow-up interview where I was asked some unexpected and concerning questions. Upon further reflection, I realized that both references had provided incorrect dates, inaccurate details about my work, and even made negative remarks about me.

I later reached out to one of them to understand what happened. His response was dismissive—he simply said he had held many jobs and might have "missed something." He didn’t show any regret, despite knowing how much damage his reference may have caused.

To make matters worse, both of these individuals have since been fired from the companies where I worked under them.

My Questions:
Is there any way I recover from their bad references for this job?

Is there any way for me to find out exactly what my references wrote or said?

Can I contact my former employers (HR or another manager) to request a formal reference letter instead?

How should I handle reference checks going forward, considering that these two managers have now damaged my credibility despite previously being supportive?

What steps can I take to recover from this situation and protect my reputation in future job applications?

Additional Context:

I’m in the early stages of my career, so professional references are especially important to me.

I feel incredibly discouraged that people I trusted could negatively impact my future, especially after they gave me positive feedback during and after my time working with them.

items.title: Adjusting my degree title slightly for clarity, would this be flagged by hiring managers?
items.human_voice:
I have a niche question, and advice from persons working in Hiring would be much appreciated. I am studying a degree officially titled: Materials science, Industrial Engineering and Management. (I do not study in an English speaking country)

I want to know if I can write this on my resume/cv as:

Bachelor of Science in Industrial Engineering and Management

Specialisation in Materials Science

or something along those lines, because according to the official study regulations, this is an Industrial Engineering and Management program with a focus on Materials Science. My personal theory is that the long, weird english name is used by the school for marketing reasons.

Would the version I use on my resume/cv be seen as dishonest, because it is not a 1 to 1 copy? I worry about background checks should I apply abroad.

items.title: Starting work in Switzerland and surprised by a very minimal contract. Normal practice or huge red flag?
items.human_voice:
I just received a job offer from a Swiss company. I’m now reviewing the contract, and to my surprise, it’s extremely simple. Single page and a few sentences. It only lists: Job Title and Employment type (Permanent), Start date, Trial period, Working hours, and Salary. And that’s it... This isn’t my first job, and in my previous contracts (none of them in Switzerland, to be clear) there was always much more detail like holidays, sick leave, pension contributions, termination, non-compete clauses, raises, etc.

The company is mid-sized and established. I'm confident it's legit. So I’m simply wondering: Is this just how contracts work in Switzerland? Do they keep things short and leave the rest to standard employment law and/or collective agreements? The position looks great, but I want to be sure I'm not setting myself up for a nasty surprise in the future.

items.title: Co-worker hides deficiencies
items.human_voice:
I have a co-worker who has produced a prototype-level project, but keeps making documentation that makes it look like his project is solid.

I am called to work with him on it, and it is tense because it feels like he is actively trying to mislead managers about his work quality.

I am called to contribute to the project being more knowledgeable than him, but I feel I don't have authority to check in any code changes I want, or do anything that might reveal the true state of things to the manager.

I am worried that I will bear the burden of the mistakes in terms of workload and blame without receiving credit.

What is a good way to deal with this?

items.title: How do I push back on an impossible scope?
items.human_voice:
I’m a relatively new developer at my current company. Recently, management decided to cancel a very expensive software license that another department heavily relies on. Instead of renewing it, they’ve tasked us (2 developers) with rebuilding the functionality from scratch.

The issue is that the technical documentation we’ve been given is basically non-existent, and the scope of the project keeps growing every time we discuss with the other department to understand the use-cases.

The official deadline for delivery is the end of this year, but with the current resources and requirements, that feels completely unfeasible. Even after putting together a MoSCoW list (must-haves, should-haves, could-haves, won’t-haves), the timeline still looks unrealistic. Both the deadline and resources are not open for discussion.

My question is: how can I communicate this effectively to my boss, who is also the more experienced developer on the project? He does not understand there is an issue with the timeline.

items.title: Advice on poor communication with a manager
items.human_voice: I'm an employee in my workplace for about 1.5 years. My boss encourages questions, yet, every time I ask a question, they act like its inconvenient and responds rudely. At other times, they will leave me on read for days (because they claim they are busy with other work responsibilities). I'm seeking on how I should move forward if I want to enjoy working in this role.

items.title: How to change team's focus without undermining boss's direction
items.human_voice:
I am the team lead for a small software company. Over the many years I've worked for the company I have highlighted many technical aspects which we need to improve in order to be more efficient, create better products, be more resilient, etc.

However a lot of my recommendations never get the green light because the boss prioritises work that directly results in more revenue, i.e: the devs should spend their time on the client projects instead of investing some time our internal tooling, etc. I understand this, but my argument is that if we invest in ourselves now we will reap the benefits long term.

The boss acknowledges the benefits of my suggestions but is very hesitant to allow the team some time to work on them. His point of view is:

it would take too much time to implement some of these changes
it introduces too much "new stuff" that the team has to learn
it introduces too much complexity

While some of the changes would indeed introduce new tools, new libraries, etc, I would argue that the more dangerous alternative is that the team stagnates and falls behind industry best practices. Moreover, the team will never learn anything new. This is profoundly sad to me, especially as a lot of the team is relatively young and these are the years of their career where they need to be exposed to lots of different things so that they gain lots of experience.

IMO the boss is afraid to embrace new tech because he no longer has the time to invest to learn how it works. He doesn't like losing oversight over the tech stack.

How can I diplomatically use the "ask for forgiveness, not permission" ethos in this case? I was planning on simply carrying out some of these changes in my spare time because once the boss sees the final product he is less likely to reject it. How do I approach my team to assist me in this without undermining the boss?

items.title: How do I best jump ship when I had issues with my supervisor and they wish to fire me? What else can I learn from it?
items.human_voice:
I had an internship this summer, and things seemed OK at the start. However, I received a PIP, allegedly for designing educational programs "not aligned with [company name]" with no details, and for being late by 1-2 minutes a few times. I had medical evidence and other supporting evidence explaining why I was late, but they dismissed it. My supervisor attempted to downplay it as simply "concerns" but I felt uncomfortable and decided to start a research project that they approved. Secretly I made my own plans to do research with professors elsewhere as I felt very uncomfortable.

Then a few days later the supervisor raised "a few things not indicating attention", a very minor "mistake" as part of the PIP. I felt increasingly uncomfortable and merely said what I needed to say, nothing more, as I felt he could use what I say against me.

I was about to resign when the supervisor informed me it was an HR decision to terminate me, reasons with few details and no transparency. A guest reported I allegedly used "inappropriate language" with no details—obviously I cannot comment on this but this is not in my character and I believe I did not do that. He also said how the company "does not need evidence" to terminate me because it was not a "court".

Should I have resigned the moment I received the PIP? I did all the PIP said in a (probably) misguided attempt to delay things. Should I have thought of backup plans in case something goes terribly wrong at the job or the supervisor has personal issues with you?

items.title: How can I explain 15 years no work history on my resume as a NEET?
items.human_voice:
I have been a NEET ("Not in Education, Employment, or Training", a person who is unemployed and not receiving an education or vocational training) for the past 15 years. I was in university for a few years after graduating high school, failed out, and moved in with my parents with whom I have lived ever since. I have not worked in all this time because frankly I had no desire to, and because my parents enabled me I enjoyed living a relatively comfortable life with no adult responsibilities.

I am now looking for work and need to explain why I have not been employed for so long. I've been aware that my lifestyle could not last forever and I've mentally prepared for this moment, and I'm confident that I'm capable of doing work and holding a job.

I've seen advice to just be honest, but I find it hard to believe my situation could be spun in any positive way. The most I could honestly offer is that I take care of some household responsibilities, like grocery shopping and taking the pets to the vet because my parents are elderly and I've begun doing some things for them. I had a couple work-study jobs in university that I did reliably, but that was so long ago I don't have references for them and frankly I don't think my supervisors would even remember me. I have been capable of hard work in the past, for example I graduated from high school with honors and made the dean's list with a 4.0 in my first semester at university, but I don't have any other noteworthy accomplishments or experience.

I'm obviously not looking for any significant position. I'll happily take a job at McDonald's or Walmart if they'll have me, but I fear my history is so bad even they'll turn me down. I do not have a car so I cannot do Uber or food delivery.

I'm considering just making something up as I've heard gaps aren't as big a deal for entry-level jobs, but I've also heard that lying can come back to bite you.

items.title: Regressions in potty-training
items.human_voice:
This summer we went through potty-training with our daughter (26 months at the time). I had the feeling it was still a bit early for her (she wasn't showing much interest) but decided to do it anyway because it was a moment where I could be close to her and give her a lot of care and attention. She picked up easily enough and in 3-4 weeks she was diaperless. We used to take her out, at the park, in the car for longish trips without issue. She was staying dry during afternoon naps and most nights too.

Then in September she went back to daycare (she went last year too and never had any issues there) and she had a massive regression. We were expecting a bit of going backwards but it's been massive, she would not hold anything at all and wet herself even every 1/2h. Together with the daycare staff we tried to hold the line and not going back to diapers when she's awake (we had to put the nappies back for the afternoon and night) but in the end it was untenable and back to diapers she went. I still tried to keep her without at home in the afternoon because I felt badly for her to let her lose a competence that way.

However, a couple of weeks ago I kept her at home for a few days because she had a bad cold and by the end of the week she was back to the level she was at this summer. She would hold the pee for much longer, tell me if she needed to poo or pee and when I took her she would be dry/clean and go in the toilet. In short it seemed like it had "clicked" with her and she was toilet trained again and out of the regression.
Then she went back to daycare and, in 4 days time, she was regressing again as badly as before. She regularly poos in her pants every day and wets herself multiple times in a few hours span.

I am at my wits end and I don't know what to do. The daycare seems clearly to be the problem, but she does not show any obvious issue there. She seems to go happily enough, she doesn't cry and when we go and fetch her she is playing happily with the other kids.
More context: she is our second child, she is a very good-natured girl, she was always calm, kind and well-adapted (unlike her older brother) even though now she is entering the terrible twos and it shows in many respects.

Has anybody gone through something similar? Do you have any suggestions?

items.title: 10 year old dealing with ADHD or Autism-like symptoms and introducing management techniques
items.human_voice:
I need to lead this with the fact that there is no official diagnosis yet - this is merely initial comparisons made by school counsellors.

So it has been suggested that my 10 year old son is dealing with a lack of awareness regarding:

understanding his emotions, and emotional expression - he gets visibly frustrated/angry at things, but claims he is "fine".
recognising certain behaviours; he claims he is being bullied "by everyone" for being "weird", when he has a rather intense energy, especially when his emotions are heightened; has very little to no spacial awareness, often getting very close to others; and acting like a "puppy" with any one he looks up to/treats him nicely (getting close, assuming a happy "begging" stance). This is more common with strangers or acquaintances, rather than close friends or relatives, and primarily adults (perhaps figures of authority?).
recognising his own contributions to conflicts. For example, he may be frustrated at something, and an unrelated input may frustrate him further, causing him to lash out, and causing a conflict. When the person affected retaliates, that's when there is a problem - he "did nothing", and they acted out towards him for "no reason".
He prefers natural light, (preferring darker light levels) over artificial light, and can get easily overstimulated with light levels, noise and cramped conditions
Constant pacing when unoccupied, unless interrupted. He again sees nothing wrong with this behaviour, even though this consistently leads to frustration of having nothing to do, and not wanting to do anything, aside from constant screen time (Minecraft or Mario Kart, YouTube, iPad games, etc).
Impulse control is a big one - constantly stealing snacks and drinks, or to play games or on his iPad, and makes efforts to wake up early (setting his alarm for 5.30) in order to attempt this, or actively hides his actions (usually by hiding the evidence in his room).
When he has trouble sleeping, he simply turns lights on, regardless of how many times he is told not to do this, and ask for music or grey/white noise (rain sounds or running water) instead, which to relax him and keep him calm, rather than keep him more awake.
Constant asking for the same things, only remembering when he has been told "later", and never when he has been told "no".

Efforts we have made to help or control this (as well as suggestions we have been given):

fidget toys, and to encourage their use when calm, to help create a sense of calming for when he is agitated
physical activity, like running around, kicking a ball, jumping on the trampoline, which he often refuses. He is currently enrolled in a martial arts class once a week, which he very much enjoys, but when it's suggested he practice his "set" at home, he refuses as well.
reading to help calm before bed (has only recently been getting into one book, which has been difficult in the past), but he only does this when he wants to, when he is not in the "bored" mindset.
limiting screen time; we do currently limit screen time to 1 hour, regardless of type and end all screen time half an hour before bed, but allow more over the weekend, extending it to a few hours depending on what is happening.
talking him through conflicts and helping him become aware of his own actions, emotions and expressions, however this often causes him to become more upset, leading him to blame and put himself down.

These are only new adjustments, so the resistances and responses are understandable, and we have been told that he will struggle with these behaviours throughout his teenage years. We do have another 12 year old who is beginning to enter his teenage phase, already reaching puberty, dealing with peer pressures, his own obsessions and resistance to rules and restrictions, etc., making this new adjustment particularly straining on us as parents.

Are there any tactics we can employ to help adopt these techniques?

Additionally, I want to introduce him to the concept of his antics. As an example, I have Epilepsy, and before this diagnosis when I was 25 (roughly 10 years ago), I was unable to understand what was going on - a lack of focus, or an inability to comprehend conversation at times; getting "dizzy spells" and nausea, and lapses in memory. Once I received this diagnosis, these symptoms made sense, making it less frustrating and easier to manage and adjust.

Introducing him to his (potential) condition may help his understanding, but I am hesitant because this diagnosis is not official (we are waiting on an appointment with a Paediatrician), and the potential of identifying as "Autistic". Again, as an example, I see my self as "myself; with Epilepsy" - this is not who I am as a person, this is just an aspect of my physiology, in the same way that I am shortsighted - I simply need to manage this; as opposed to "being an Epileptic", and defining my life through these restrictions.

I want to ask if I should do this, though that will potentially draw opinions - I am uncertain. But if I do, how should I go about this with a young, impressionable mind?

items.title: Is time really the only solution for a child with attachment issues?
items.human_voice:
My partner and I have a 3 year old biological son and a foster 3 year old girl that's been full-time with us for 10 months. I'll gloss over the details, but I have never developed any attachment nor have I felt love for the little girl. I have still acted as a dad for her as best as I could, but it has drained me and I've had a burnout. As a result I told my partner that I would stop being responsible for her, and minimize my time around her, until I figure a way to not be so unhappy in her presence. My partner lives with her mother and I live 5 mins away, we've always been both quite independent of each other - so this arrangement is something that works for us currently.

Obviously things could be better. I see my partner and my son less as a result of this arrangement. If I can manage to spend time with this little girl without being mentally exhausted, it's all the better for everyone. I see three ways this could happen:

I somehow become able to tolerate the behavioral issues of this little girl
We find a way to discipline her so she behaves
She begins feeling securely attached

On (1): I don't have any idea of how to proceed. I am able to stay cool in the face of the occasional tantrums from my son. But when it comes from her, I am way more susceptible. She is constantly demanding for attention in whatever way possible and it drives me crazy. Without feeling attached to her, I don't see how I could withstand that on a regular basis. Even if I were to work on some anger management, it wouldn't help with the mental exhaustion. I have been thinking of therapy but I don't see exactly which kind, considering that my reaction is fairly normal.

On (2): I am biased but I think that the way I do it works. I am caring but strict. I will give her affection during bonding time, and never when she asks for it in an excessive or inappropriate manner. After a couple of months together, she has come to behave like a regular child when I am alone with her, and I can tolerate her then. But it only works if it's just the two of us. My partner is not as strict, as her attachment to her is different and as she does not want to feel cruel in difficult times. This little girl knows that and she will regularly push my partner to the extreme so she can get attention. When we're looking from professional advice, we essentially get told to bear with it. That we should tell her that her behavior is inappropriate and that she matters to us without needing her to draw our attention to us. But isolating her as punishment is supposedly a no-no, and that's the only thing I can do not to go insane. We've been following these guidelines for weeks, and I don't see any change happening in her.

On (3): I have tried many things. I read a book on attachment issues. We've been to parent-child bonding activities together. We've seen quite a few professionals. Still, this girl is only preoccupied by whether her foster mom or dad are paying attention to her. We've been told that 10 months living with us is nothing, that it'll take many more years to maybe get there. I am in denial about that. I refuse to believe that there isn't a way a child who has been separated from her parents can chill out with her new family after a couple of months. How ridiculous is the human condition that a child with attachment issues will do precisely the things that put them at risk of not being kept in their foster family? I get that she's testing us but to what point? It's not helping her situation.

A couple of notes:

My partner sees this child as her own, and has no plans of sending her away ever.
I make no bets in what the future will be. I could get attached to this girl. I could also not be attached, but become able to tolerate her. The current arrangement I have with my partner could last also a long time.
There are currently no tensions with the way things are. All four of us are doing ok. Given our way of life, there would be nothing to gain in a proper separation with my partner.

July 2025 edit: Thanks to everyone who replied, I have carefully read your answers and truly appreciate them. I want to add some context:

The situation has evolved so that we spend more time together as 4, but it remains that I am not feeling serene, connected, attached to our girl. My "attachment" to her is unfortunately conditional: when she acts like a normal little girl I am happy to have her around, but when all she does is seek out our attention, I just wish she'd be gone. I do my best to treat her equally to my son, with whom I have such an easy time feeling compassion for.
I have autism. A lot of you picked up on the fact that I speak rather coldly and bluntly about the situation, and you've hit home. I have this very emotionally detached manner of speaking about my life, but the good news is that it paints a darker image than what actually is. It's difficult to reason about my attachment with our girl and to put myself in her shoes. My autism is definitely a large part of the equation, and it's hard to figure out whether it will be at all possible for me to bond with her, even following the good advice I have been given here and in therapy. But I can't just rule it out on that basis.
Becoming a foster parent was initially something I wanted to "try", and despite being warned early on that there was no such thing as trying a child, I played along with my partner who was deeply willing to be a foster parent. It was the second day I visited our little girl that I realized it would be very difficult for me, and my partner was not at all ready to turn back then. We had several arguments and the decision was very difficult to make. I have considered leaving my partner months later, but we love eachother very much, so I stuck around best as I could.

items.title: How to navigate a 2 year old saying "stop it" to everyone
items.human_voice:

Recently however I told her when she wants daddy to stop tickling her she should say "Stop" or "Stop it" instead of the usual "No!"

This worked well for the games but now she will tell anyone to "Stop it!" When they walk into a room, if they're on a toy she wanted to use, literally anything and all day long.

How should I approach this?

I have been redirecting her when I can, trying to provide more words for what she's saying.

I will say things like "No, she is doing cooking right now and can't stop. What can you see her cooking?" Or "They are using the slide right now and you would like a turn? Let's wait here for our turn."

items.title: How to help 13 year old to be more open, motivated and responsible
items.human_voice:
I have a son - 13 yrs old. He is doing well in his school gifted in both Math and Language arts.
But he has a few behavioral / personality issues that seem to be bothering us especially now since he is reaching his puberty age and looking for more independence.

He is not particularly strong willed. He tried a few things and giving up as soon as he think it is too hard for him. For ex. I enrolled him in karate class at the age of 6, he reached very close to black belt but now left it since he is finding it too hard.
He is too picky in eating, small for his age and he seems to have accepted it that he is different from his peers but at the same time he also feels inferior that he is small and not as strongly built as his peers.
He is not physically too active, he likes to lie around play games or watch vidoes from his favorite youtube channel and gets less involved in physical activities. To motivate him, we got a table tennis table, pickle ball set, swimming twice a week, tennis classes, badminton etc. And I encourage him to come join with me and his younger brother playing these games and other board games and family activities but none of these interests him.
Till now he used to read a lot but now he also lost interest in reading.
The biggest issue now I am facing is he is not motivated to do anything. He has in front of him his 2 yr younger brother who is so much into trying all sorts of things, trying all kinds of technical things including building his own gaming PC, building custom RC cars, trying all kinds of other STEM experiments his age. I am mentioning his younger brother not to compare both of them but just that his yonger brothers example in front of him doesnt work to motivate him. However whatever little he helped his yonger brother do his stuff, he is quick to take credit for what he did.
He doesnt have friends his age, he talks and likes to hang around with his younger brothers friends. This might be linked to the point 2 above.
He has strong attitude problem which is why he is not a type someone would like to be aroud with. Very quick to blame others for something wrong that happened with him, not willing to take responsibility for his own choices. Likes to argue when you try to talk to him about what he needs to work on or improve upon. Recently his tennis coach complained that he tried to talk to him about what he needs to improve upon, but instead of working on his mistake he argued about what his coach did wrong.
Clumsy. I have to keep reminding him about tying his shoe laces, brushing his teeth, combing his hairs, cleaning his room etc. He is very forgetful and keeps missing his basic chores.

items.title: 2 y/o with speech delay
items.human_voice:
My son turned 2 in April. He is currently in early intervention for speech, they also are working on his receptive language.

When he was 10 months old he got ear tubes after having ear infections for several months. After his tubes were placed we felt like he stopped responding to us, when we called his name or yelled he wouldn’t look. We were concerned about his hearing for several months following the surgery and he couldn’t get through the first hearing test he had but was able to pass at his 2 year appointment. The ear doctor said that his ear infections and tubes had nothing to do with him not speaking but I truly felt that there was a clear difference after his surgery and when they did a pressure test on his ears at 16 months it seemed to correct the problem as he was way more responsive to us but still only saying minimal words.

Well now we have been doing EI for almost 6 months, he has developed a few more words and signs and it’s more consistent with showing us what he wants. He loves to play with his sister and cousins and seeks out other kids when we go to play group or the park. Our EI therapist said she would like to see him be more reactive to her calling his name and for him to do more imitation play although he does it with us. He also gets hyper focused on a toy or activity he is playing and will ignore you if you try to get him to do a different task or activity which I feel is a typical for some toddlers but seems to concern our EI therapist . She has also suggested having him tested for autism but we feel he is too young and everyone who meets him who understands autism or has worked with kids with autism feel that he doesn’t show the typical signs. I should add that he makes eye contact, interacts with other kids and adults that he knows well or even has only met a few times, he also is entering the two year old tantrum stage but it never lasts over 5 minutes if that and he is redirectable.

I am curious peoples thoughts on waiting for testing or giving him more time to develop. He is also starting daycare in a few weeks which will be two full days every week. I just feel there is so much pressure to label kids and it’s becoming very overwhelming for my husband and myself as we do all the suggestions given to us and have seen progress but wish he was saying more. Thank you for any suggestions or words of encouragement.

items.title: How to make 11 years old kid do homework
items.human_voice:
I have an 11 years old daughter who goes to a fairly "laid back" school - in particular they didn't use to have homework regularly. Occasionally she brought back some exercises that she did immediately after coming home - but this was maybe once every two months. However, recently she got a new teacher who insist on giving homework every week, for the weekend - and I have really hard time to make her do her homework. Apparently all of her classmates do the homework in the school in the afternoon, but she prefers to play instead.

She complains that it's unfair that her younger siblings don't have homework. I tried to motivate her positively ("If you do your homework, you get cookies"), but to no avail. I tried to motivate her negatively ("If you don't finish your homework, you can't watch TV.", "If you don't do your homework, don't get good grades, won't succeed in life."), but it just lead to "Right, I'm going to stab myself with a knife, because I don't want to live if I have to do homework. You don't love me anyway because you want me to do homework.". Although I think she's overdramatising (there was a kind of "psychological checkup" at school and the psychiatrist said she doesn't suffer from depression), there was suicide in the family, so her choice of words does scare me. Also sometimes she does her homework without me asking here - my problem is that when she doesn't do it, I can't motivate her.

The problem is unfortunately a little more generic: I also have problem motivating her to go outside, go to an excursion, walk the dog, check out a kids-specific exhibition at a museum, etc. Sometimes she gets into this state of mind ("I hate the world, especially you!") where I simply can't reach her and she's not willing to do anything.

I'm a little loss at here. My wife says it's "normal teen stuff", but due to her work schedule she's often not at home at the same time as the kids, so can't help me. I've googled and found a few ideas:

Set aside a specific time to do her homework. She'd just go to her own room and do nothing or read a book.
Let her do the homework while I'm doing some chores, so she sees she's not the only one who works. She'd just go to her own room and do nothing or read a book.

I don't remember from my childhood that I had this much trouble with homework - I used get over it quickly, so I could play. Do you have any better ideas?

items.title: 6 year old won't go to the bathroom by herself anymore, because of being scared. What to do?
items.human_voice:

Every day is either the best or worst day ever, and she usually declares each day as one or the other multiple times per day. Everything is an emergency when it comes up, she wants our full attention all of the time even when we can't give it, talks a lot, and screams and yells a lot. Just to paint a picture.

Yesterday, she started asking about if anything lives in the toilet and can come out while she is using it. We told her there is not. She told us about a noise that came from the bathroom when she turned on the faucet or something, which makes sense because I had had the water to the house off earlier that day for some repair work and some pretty intense gurgling afterwards is normal. Despite our explanations of why that sound occurred, she is scared of bugs or animals coming out of the toilet while she is peeing.

Right now, she is complaining about being scared of going to the bathroom, and has been crying about it for 10 minutes. We've explained to her that everything is fine and there's nothing to be afraid of. Last night, I helped her go to the bathroom when she was scared, thinking that would be the end of that, but it apparently is not. We've decided to not continue going with her to the bathroom, so that this doesn't become a regular thing, and she absolutely refuses to go.

She was also one difficult to potty train. It took probably about two or two and a half years (from the time she was two and a half) for her to stop wetting herself regularly, and even now she goes through phases where she regularly pees in her underwear a little bit before going to the bathroom.

items.title: My 10mnd old wants 100% of the time attention, how can I reduce this?
items.human_voice:
My 10mnd old demands 100% of the time attention from others other than his parents, how can I reduce this?

When I or his mom are around, he can play somewhat solo. I give him attention for a significant amount of time, but also want to practice playing solo. I dont expect 100% independency, he can entertain himself about an hour or so, but we do need to be close by.

His mother and both his grandmothers experience the same thing.

However, when we bring him to the daycare and pick him up at the end of a day, we get the feedback that he has been practising for tornado siren all day (he has a good set of lungs), unless they give full attention, which they cant because there are more kids.

This is coming to the point where the daycare is dropping hints that they might not be able to do this for a lot longer. Their main argument is that this can't be fun for him and while its not really a problem now, this might soon turn in an a bad experience permanently. The guardian there has been doing this for about 30 years and she says he is one of the most difficult cases she's ever had.

He is like that with more people. My father (who's better with kids 2yrs+) has difficulty with him too. My kid can be (and is often) described as pretty intense. It is very obvious wether or not he is liking something, he is happy with the same intensity.

I'm looking for something we can do. My first though was to "leave" (e.g. do laundry a small distance over) him for 5mins, then come back. Then increase that more and more.

When he is at the daycare, he will not stop crying at all. Practicing this has booked us no results at all.

We've asked all people babysitting him to practice this and they all do, and it works for them, as long as there are no others to share attention with.

When the daycare guardian picks him up and gives the attention, he stops crying immediatly, I'm confident he sees her as a safe person too. The guardian suggests that he might be overstimulated because when the other kids go to bed, he becomes easier. But when I ask if she then gives him more private attention, the answer is yes. Me and his mother also are not really under the impression that overstimulation is the issue, as we bring him to more situations where there is plenty of stimuli, and he doesnt really seem to impressed by it. He also like a bit more wild playing, such as swings, or placing him on one of the kid cars and drive him around.

His week is like so:

Monday: His mother has him (private attention, but then he plays well enough)
Tuesday: Daycare, significant crying when left alone (even for a few seconds!)
Wednesday: His mother has him (private attention, but then he plays well enough)
Tuesday: His grandmother has him (private attention, but then he plays well enough)
Friday: I have him (private attention, but then he plays well enough)
Weekend: I and his mother have him (private attention, but then he plays well enough)

We're out of ideas how to approach this and we need the daycare to work. Does anyone know a good technique we can try?

My mother described me the same when I was young, easy but continues, she left me to cry and that seemed to work for me, but when my kid is with us, no real issues. And letting him cry does nothing for the daycare.

He has no issues with sleeping, wherever he is. At the daycare he becomes so upset he barely eats/drinks, worsening everything.

Little addendum: The daycare is very much in line with our philosophy. She takes them outside often, lets them play in the rain (she has raincoats) and stomp in puddles (she has boots). She promotes creative behaviour (like couloring), they sing together (I dont like singing, but its a fun kid activity). She is not a neatfreak, not scared of a booger etc, but does care about hygiene to a realistic standard. She is of the "emphisise positive, redirect negative" style (unless something serieusly wrong), creating self esteem. We do that too.

items.title: In 2025 tax return, should I use numbers from the original or amended 2024 return if 2024 amendmend is not accepted yet?
items.human_voice:
I need to amend my 2024 tax return. While this in itself does not pose a problem, this amended return is not likely to be accepted until much later than the 2025 return due date.

Therefore, my 2025 tax return will be processed by the IRS before my 2024 amendment will.

In my situation, the 2024 return does affect the numbers in 2025, because I have AMT tax credit carryforward (form 8801), so this amount changes in 2025's form 8801 with 2024 amendment. To be precise, the final tax amount that I owe for 2025 should not change, since I got enough credit, but the amount that I carry forward will (which should affect the future 2026 return).

So how should I proceed?

Option 1 would be to use numbers from the amended 2024 return, so the numbers in 2025 form 8801 are correct. But could IRS reject this return based on the discrepancy with the original return that they already processed?

Option 2 would be to use numbers from the original return, in which case there would be no conflict between the currently processed 2024 return and the new 2025 return. But in this case I'd have to amend 2025 return once my 2024 amendment is processed, which is an unnecessary hassle for all parties involved.

I tried to search online, but the only kind of answers that I've found was that 2024 is not related to 2025. Unfortunately, this is not true in my case, where the numbers in 2025 do depend on 2024 return.

items.title: Macaulay Duration formula not making sense
items.human_voice:
I am currently studying annuities, stocks, and bonds for an exam, and I came across this question about Modified/Macauly Duration. The problem reads:

A portfolio contains three bonds, all of which have par value $1000. The first has a two-year term and no coupons, the second is a three-year bond with no coupons, and the third is a two-year 6% bond with semiannual coupons. If each bond is purchased to yield 5% convertible semiannually, find the modified duration of the portfolio.

This is the problem's solution:

P_I = 1000v^4 = 905.95

P_{II} = 1000v^6 = 862.30

P_{III} = 30v + 30v^2 + 30v^3 + 1030v^4 = 1018.81

MacD(III) = (0.5·30v + 1·30v^2 + 1.5·30v^3 + 2·
1030v^4)/1018.81 = 1.9152

MacD_P = (2P_I + 3P_{II} + 1.9152P_{III})/(P_I + P_{II} + P_{III})

= 2.2784

ModD_P = v * 2.2784 = 2.2228

The solution is quite confusing to me because the normal Macauly duration formula is:

items.title: Does this substack article on "the illusion of diversification" make sense?
items.human_voice:
This posting on substack uses much terminology about dot products and wedge products that will not be understood by most non-mathematicians, but the idea is something like this: Suppose two stocks usually either rise or fall together, or if one of them usually rises when the other falls, or if 3 times the price of the first stock minus 4 times the price of the second stock plus 2 times the price of the third stock typically rises when the fourth stock rises, etc., etc., then you have less diversity than if all the stocks behaved independently of each other. That part seems clear enough.

The simplest and most extreme case of this is an investor whose portfolio is two shares of one company, but he thinks they are shares of two different companies. Clearly he has less diversity than if they were shares of two unrelated companies.

The author goes on to say that if "your assets are linearly dependent," then "They are trapped on a 2D plane. You are infinitely exposed to any risk factor perpendicular to that plane. You have Phantom Diversification."

Understanding that requires a bit of math, but in that "simplest and most extreme case" mentioned above the "plane" in which you are "trapped" is that in which the two stock prices will always be equal, and the "risk factor perpendicular to that plane" is the price of the first stock minus the price of the second stock.

This ignorant investor does not know that the price of the first stock minus the price of the second will never fluctuate and will always remain zero. It seems to me that if he is thus "infinitely exposed" to some "risk factor", it must be because of his ignorance of the fact that the two shares he owns are both of the same company.

So my question is this: How would someone take advantage of his ignorance of that fact by buying something from him or selling something to him, in a way that would not be possible if he knew that his two shares were both of the same company?

items.title: Would you buy real estate equity at a 15% discount if there was ZERO rental income? (Hypothetical Structure)
items.human_voice:
I’m looking for some brutal feedback on a real estate deal structure I’m debating with a partner. We are trying to figure out if this would actually appeal to passive investors or if the lack of cash flow makes it a non-starter.

Here is the premise: You invest in an owner-occupied single-family home in a strong market. The homeowner stays in the house, so there is no tenant and no monthly rent check.

Instead of cash flow, the return comes from two places: a Day-1 Discount and a "Ticking Clock" Equity kicker.

Basically, you buy $50,000 worth of equity for $42,500 (an instant 15% discount). The homeowner pays you absolutely nothing monthly—no interest, no rent.

However, to protect you from being stuck forever, there is a "Ratchet" clause. If the homeowner hasn’t bought you out or sold the home by Year 5, your equity share automatically increases by 10% per year. This effectively dilutes the homeowner and motivates them to refinance or sell without us having to force a foreclosure.

The math we are modeling looks like this: If you invest $42.5k today and the home appreciates 4% a year, by Year 5 your share is worth roughly $61k. That’s about an $18.5k profit (43% total return) without ever dealing with a tenant or a toilet. If they stay longer than 5 years, that "Ratchet" kicks in and you start owning more of the house for free, compounding the return.

The Question: As an investor, would you touch this?

On one hand, it feels like a zero-coupon bond backed by hard assets—I get real estate exposure at a discount. On the other hand, it’s illiquid. I’m stuck until they sell or refinance.

Is a 15% discount enough to make you wait 5 years for your money? Or would you need a bigger discount to touch a non-cash-flowing asset?

items.title: Nonresident alien with U.S.-source §988 gain: ECI, FDAP, or not taxable?
items.human_voice:
Facts

• Taxpayer is a nonresident alien who does not meet the substantial presence test but lives and works in the U.S.

• After moving to the U.S. and establishing a U.S. tax home through employment, the taxpayer converts foreign personal savings (e.g., EUR) to USD.

• The foreign currency represents personal savings accumulated over multiple prior years; upon conversion, the USD amount realized exceeds the taxpayer’s basis determined under §988 due solely to exchange-rate movements.

• The resulting foreign currency gain is ordinary income under §988.

Sourcing

Under §865, foreign currency gain is sourced by the taxpayer’s residence, and residence is determined by tax home under §911(d)(3).
Because the taxpayer’s principal place of business is in the U.S., the §988 gain appears to be U.S.-source income.

Issue: How is this §988 gain taxed to a nonresident alien?

Analysis

• The gain does not appear to be effectively connected income (ECI): it arises from personal savings and is not connected to a U.S. trade or business; the taxpayer’s U.S. employment is not a material factor in producing the gain.

• The gain also does not appear to be FDAP income:

Under Reg. §1.988-3(c)(1), exchange gain or loss on a §988 transaction is not treated as interest, except in limited,

specifically enumerated cases (e.g., certain tax-exempt bonds, integrated debt hedges).
The §988 regulations treat the conversion of nonfunctional currency as a sale or other disposition of property, applying §1001 amount-realized and basis mechanics.
Gains from sales or other dispositions of property are excluded from FDAP under Reg. §1.1441-2(b)(2)(i).

Question

If the gain is U.S.-source but is neither ECI nor FDAP, is it correct that the §988 gain is not taxable to the nonresident alien under §871, notwithstanding its ordinary character?
