items.title: What is the "breakeven" annual rent such that you would buy it if the rent exceeds this amount?
items.human_voice:
Question: Suppose you currently rent an apartment and have an option to buy it for $200,000. Property taxes are $2,000 per year and are deductible for income tax purposes. Annual maintenance costs on the property are $1,500 per year and are not tax deductible. You expect property taxes and maintenance costs to increase at the rate of inflation. Your income tax rate is 40%, you can earn an after-tax real interest rate of 2% per year, and you plan to keep the apartment forever. What is the "breakeven" annual rent such that you would buy it if the rent exceeds this amount?

Solution: $6,700 per year

My confusion stems from reading

you can earn an after-tax real interest rate of 2% per year

This throws me off because the solution is what I would pay per year in property tax and maintenance cost if I buy the house. I am not earning anything. I'm paying. I'm having difficulty understanding why should I multiply the PV cost of owning by 2%. Does it mean that if you were to invest the $335,000 at a 2% rate you will earn $6,700 per year or would you rather pay $6,700 every year for the rest of your life by choosing to own the house?

Full solution:

The after-tax annual outlay from the purchase is:
1500 + (100%−40%) ∗2000 = $2, 700

The present value of this perpetuity is: 2700/2% = $135, 000

The present value of the costs of owning are:
135000 + 200000 = $335, 000

The break-even rent is: 2% ∗335000 = $6, 700 per year.

items.title: Why isn't the "erase and replace" strategy routine for avoiding estimated payments and delaying taxes (for married retirees with IRAs, at least)?
items.human_voice:
Assume that a retired, married U.S. couple receives capital gains, possibly erratic, throughout the year for whatever reason.

The prevailing recommendation is to complete IRS Form 2210 Schedule AI throughout the year* to calculate estimated tax payments and to make these payments in a timely manner to avoid penalties. The (sometimes needless**) payments represent money that's no longer available to earn income.

As an alternative, consider the "erase and replace" approach, in which withholding from an IRA rollover is used to satisfy the required payments. (1, 2, 3, 4.) (The IRS considers withholding at any point in the year to be distributed evenly over the four payment periods.) In this strategy, the couple makes zero estimated payments throughout the year and then performs an indirect IRA rollover each December in the amount of 90% of that year's tax or 100-110% of last year's tax (depending on their AGI), whichever is less. It's arranged that 100% of the rollover is withheld for federal taxes; the rollover is completed soon after with cash. An indirect rollover is permitted every 12 months per person; to avoid having the date creep forward when meeting this requirement, the couple alternates between rollovers for each person, resulting in ~24 months spacing.

Thus,

Federal tax is considered to be paid in a timely manner,
No penalties are incurred,
Form 2210 can potentially be ignored, and
Instead of making estimated payments (which may be refunded anyway, as described below), that money can be used to earn income starting as early as April 15 (the deadline for the first estimated payment) to the rollover replacement date (as @littleadv indicates, this minimizes the amount of time the rollover money is absent from the IRA).

Note that this strategy addresses federal tax only; state laws vary regarding withholding and estimated payments.

I see no indication that this approach is recommended for routine use, so either there's an error or it's an obscure edge case (although it doesn't seem unusual for a retired couple to both have IRAs and also receive capital gains). I appreciate your comments.

*Example of a "gotcha" if the couple doesn't complete Form 2210 Schedule AI throughout the year: The couple receives capital gains of $125K in January and then unexpected capital gains of $125K more in December. They spend most of the year paying zero estimated taxes, as their January income is tax free under the standard deduction and 0% capital gains bracket. In December, when they turn out to owe tax on $250K capital gains for the year, Schedule AI reveals retrospectively that the required first-period estimated payment is the lesser of 1/4 of 90% of this year's tax, or 1/4 of 100-110% of last year's tax (depending on their AGI), or 22% of the tax on first-period-annualized 4 × $125K = $500K (Schedule AI, part I, lines 1-21). None of these numbers is zero, and so a penalty is incurred. (Discussed in this answer, described as the "gold standard" on the topic, and in this answer and this one.)

**Example of a needless payment: Wary of the "gotcha" described above, the couple makes an estimated payment in the first period. If no more capital gains are received after January, however, the federal tax ends up being zero after all, and that payment is refunded in full in the following year, representing a loss in potential investment income.

According to the Senate's own summary of Secure 2.0 (italics added for emphasis):

Section 109, Higher catch-up limit to apply at age 60, 61, 62, and 63. Under current law,
employees who have attained age 50 are permitted to make catch-up contributions under a
retirement plan in excess of the otherwise applicable limits. The limit on catch-up contributions
for 2021 is $6,500, except in the case of SIMPLE plans for which the limit is $3,000. Section 109
increases these limits to the greater of $10,000 or 50 percent more than the regular catch-up amount in 2025 for individuals who have attained ages 60, 61, 62 and 63. The increased amounts are indexed for inflation after 2025. Section 109 is effective for taxable years beginning after
December 31, 2024.

The "enhanced" catch-up limit for the 60-63 set for 2025 was $11,250. But while the base catch-up increased from $7500 to $8000 in 2026, the enhanced limit for 2026 remained $11,250, rather than rising to $12,000 (50% above the new $8K limit, matching inflation).

Why did the limit for the enhanced catch-up not increase to $12,000 (or thereabouts; the hidden factors in the inflation-adjusted and rounded value might not be exactly $12,000, but it should have increased at least a little)? The only thing I can think of is that the summary is wrong, but the full bill's changes seem to make no distinction between the raw dollar value and the computed dollar value of 50% above the regular limit when it comes to indexing for inflation:

‘In the case of a year beginning after December 31, 2025, the Secretary shall adjust annually the adjusted dollar amounts applicable under clauses (i) and
(ii) of subparagraph (E)

and clauses (i) and (ii) are the clauses that select the greater of the fixed and computed value from their respective (I) and (II) subclauses; if the indexing was only supposed to apply to the fixed dollar values, I'd think they'd say "under subclause (I) of clauses (i) and (ii) respectively of subparagraph (E)", or some other lawyerly way to more clearly specify that only the raw dollar value was indexed for inflation, not the result of the max(10000, 1.5 * base_limit). The bill text I found might be from an earlier draft (it computes the value from 150% of the 2024 limit, while the summary specifies 150% of the 2025 limit), but the other versions I'm finding (e.g. this House bill are clearly even more incorrect, setting the age ranges differently, and putting the changes in Section 108, not Section 109).

items.title: How to track the optimum time to sell stocks and buy cryptocurrency?
items.human_voice:
I have a bunch of stocks and mutual funds in my portfolio. I'd like to sell some small percent of these "traditional" investments and purchase some cryptocurrency. But I’m trying to figure out how to calculate when is the best time to do this transfer.

Basically, what I want is to see some chart and setup an alert that tells me:

When the stock price is high (relative to my fiat currency) and
When the price of the cryptocurrency is low (relative to the above fiat currency)

First, how do I do this theoretically? Is there some way to construct a chart that simplifies two lines into one line, which is some calculation of the two lines that shows a single line with points very high on the y-axis when the above two conditions are true, and very low on the y-axis when the above conditions are not true?

Second, how can I setup an alert that tells me when the chart above is at some sort of year-time-high, so I can be alerted that "now" is a good time to sell stocks and buy the given cryptocurrency.

items.title: Shortcut to getting your managed funds to weigh towards defensive stocks
items.human_voice:
There are a lot of stocks that ride out recessions better than others, but they typically underperform during boom times. Weighing a directly-managed portfolio to increase resilience is certainly doable, within limits, with the adequate knowledge, but error-prone without it. I don't have that knowledge.

Personally, I find that talking economics to the average retail investment professionals is a thankless effort, they mostly just parrot back platitudes like "not timing the market" or pooh pooh whatever concerns you have because it is not reflected in the numbers yet and focus on historical returns. I am sure there are better ones available in boutique shops, just not at my own investment levels.

Which gets me wonder: my investment questionnaires also include a mandatory question (Canada) which asks for my risk tolerance level: low, medium, high. Mine is currently at medium.

Without considering my circumstances overmuch (I can add them in comment if necessary), is downgrading to a "low risk tolerance" a good way to reshuffle to more defensive portfolios, without the need to argue for the reasons for doing so with investment advisors?

I am sitting at about 55-45 bonds/stocks, IIRC. Plan would be to pop back up to medium later, when comfortable.

items.title: What to do if the IRS doesn't know how much I owe?
items.human_voice:
I have been making regular payments towards an IRS payment plan for a couple of years. Starting maybe eight months ago, my bills started just displaying "???" as the balance due, and the Web site also just says "Balance not available" with no pay off or other details what-so-ever.

Based on my estimates from the data I have prior to the "???"'s appearing, I should be paid off, or really close, but I've seen no change in the status on-line, nor received any E-mail or mail saying its paid off, and the payments continue to be automatically withdrawn. I can shut off automatic payments, but if my math is wrong about how much I owe, I don't want to miss a payment.

I've tried the IRS on-line chat, it won't ever take me to a human. Each time I called the 1-800 number, a recording just said they don't have enough staff to handle my issue, and it doesn't even let me wait on hold. I just want to pay off any remaining amount and be done, but can't reach any human.

How can I know how much I have left?

items.title: How to perform a mass charge back against a business?
items.human_voice:
I'm in a dispute with Uber over a ton of non-delivered items. This is everything from 20 cent charges to over $100 for undelivered food.

I initially kept using them as it was infrequent and the refunds and credit they gave me covered it. However, recently they have gotten more aggressive around not issuing refunds.

Here's two good examples from ordering from McDonald's. soda spilled, in the bag, soaking my food, and the Uber support guy refused to refund me after I sent a photo of the soaking wet bag. Second one is I orderered a large meal. I received a large fry container, but the McDonald's employee used the scoop for the small fry container. Uber refused to refund the difference. Most of them are just the food was not delivered. A few is damaged food. If you pay extra for modifications you frequently do not receive the modification and Uber refuses to refund often. I'm at the point where it would take a lot of work to itemize everything Uber owes me.

It's my understanding if I file a chargeback the bank will almost always side with me. Is there a means of easily doing this for many charges?

I only use this one credit card for Uber. I no longer do business with them. How do I dispute all of the charges on my card? Would I have to write a script to fill out web forms?

Update Uber has an arbitration clause that's hard to get around. My options are either file a charge back for every 20 cent or more error they refused to refund. (I believe the bank refunds the entire order) Either that or file in arbitration court. The bank is more likely to give me a more favorable judgment, while arbitration court is more likely to favor Uber. I'll recover more money by charging back.

items.title: Marriage and inheritance / separation planning
items.human_voice:
My wife and I are both going to receive a pretty sizeable inheritance from both of our parents. The inheritance we'll both receive should be, roughly, around the same figure.

I've done some research on how to best manage this money as a couple and have discovered that in Canada, where I am, there is a post-nuptial agreement we can create to map out a plan on where the money goes and what happens if we were to ever divorce. I've also learned that once you mix the money together it's very hard to separate.

The thing is that my wife and I are in a high trust relationship, we're both kind people, and I don't suspect things would get nasty if we split up. I don't really expect us to split up at all. With that being said I don't have any concerns with mixing our money together, and if my parents pass away first I was planning on immediately maxing out both of our tax-shielded investment vehicles. And when her parents go continuing to mix our money together. We are also homeowners.

My question is: is this a reasonable avenue for us to go in our planning and what would separation of our estate look like if we weren't to create a post-nuptial agreement? Am I missing anything obvious?
